6.1.1 [α΄. Περὶ ἀβροτόνου τε καὶ ἀψινθίου καὶ τῶν ἑκατέρου εἰδῶν.] Ἀβροτόνου ταύτης τῆς πόας οὔτε τὴν ἰδέαν χρὴ γράφειν ἐπὶ τοσούτοις τε καὶ τοιούτοις ἀνδράσιν οὔτε τὰς κατὰ μέρος ἐνεργείας ὡς ἐκεῖνοι, κᾂν εἰ μὴ διωρισμένως, ἀλλὰ σαφῶς γοῦν ἐδήλωσαν. εἰρήσεται δὲ καὶ ἡμῖν ἐπιπλέον ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐν τῇ περὶ συνθέσεως φαρμάκων πραγματείᾳ καὶ τῇ τῶν εὐπορίστων, ἔστι δ’ ὅτε κᾀν τοῖς τῆς θεραπευτικῆς μεθόδου γράμμασιν, ὅταν ἡ χρεία καλῇ. μόνον δὲ, ὅπερ ἐξ ἀρχῆς πρόκειται, τὰς καθόλου δυνάμεις ἁπάντων τῶν φαρμάκων ἐπισκέψασθαι, τοῦτο κᾀπὶ τῶν ἄλλων μὲν ἕπεται, καὶ νῦν δὲ ἤδη ποιητέον αὐτὸ καὶ λεκτέον ὡς θερμόν τέ ἐστι καὶ ξηρὸν τὴν δύναμιν τὸ ἀβρότονον, ἐν τρίτῃ που τάξει καὶ ἀποστάσει μετὰ τὰς συμμετρίας τεταγμένον, διαφορητικήν τέ τινα καὶ τμητικὴν ἔχον δύναμιν. τῆς αὐτῆς δ’ ἐστὶ δυνάμεως καὶ ἡ τρίψις αὐτοῦ εἰληφυῖα, ὥσπερ τὸ σαρκωτικόν τε καὶ δακνῶδες. ὅτι δὲ καὶ ὡς πρὸς τὴν εὔκρατον φύσιν ἡ τοιαύτη τάξις ἐξετάζεται πρόσθεν εἴρηται πολλάκις. ἐξεύρομεν δ’ αὐτοῦ τὴν κρᾶσιν οὐχ ἥκιστα μὲν καὶ τῇ γεύσει τεκμηράμενοι, πικρὸν γὰρ ἱκανῶς ἐστιν. ὁ δὲ τοιοῦτος χυμὸς ἐδείκνυτο γεώδης μὲν ὢν τὴν οὐσίαν, ὑπὸ θερμότητος δαψιλοῦς λεπτύνεσθαι, ὥστε καὶ θερμαίνειν καὶ ξηραίνειν οὐκ ἀγεννῶς. οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ διωρισμένῃ πείρᾳ, περὶ ἧς ἔμπροσθεν εἴρηται πολλάκις, ἀκριβῶς βασανίσαντες ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς εὕρομεν τὸ φάρμακον τοῦτο κράσεως. εἴτε γὰρ κόψας τὴν κόμην ἅμα τοῖς ἄνθεσιν, ἄχρηστον γὰρ αὐτοῦ τὸ λοιπὸν κάρφος, ἐπιπάττοις ἕλκει καθαρῷ, δακνῶδές τε καὶ ἐρεθιστικὸν φαίνεται, εἴτε ἀποβρέξας ἐν ἐλαίῳ καταντλεῖν ἐθελήσαις ἤτοι κεφαλὴν ἢ γαστέρα, θερμαῖνον σφοδρῶς εὑρεθήσεται. καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ ὅσοι κατὰ περιόδους ἁλίσκονται ῥίγεσιν, εἰ καὶ τούτους ἀνατρίβοις πρὸ τῆς εἰσβολῆς, ἧττον ῥιγῶσιν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τὴν αἴσθησιν εὐθὺς ἅμα τῷ προσφέρεσθαι λανθάνει θερμαῖνον. ὅτι δὲ ἕλμινθας ἀναιρεῖν εἰκός ἐστι πικρὸν ὑπάρχον αὐτὸ καὶ πρὸ τῆς πείρας εὔδηλον, εἴ τι μεμνήμεθα τῶν ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων εἰρημένων ὑπὲρ τοῦ πικροῦ χυμοῦ τῆς φύσεως. εἰδήσεις δ’ εὐθὺς ὡς καὶ διαφορητικήν τινα καὶ τμητικὴν ἔχει δύναμιν. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὡς μᾶλλον ἀψινθίου τοῦτο ὑπάρχειν ἀναγκαῖον αὐτῷ συλλογίσασθαί σοι παρέσται πρῶτον μὲν ἐκ τῆς γεύσεως. ἐλαχίστης γάρ τινος μετέχει στρυφνότητος τὸ ἀβρότονον, ἀψίνθιον δὲ οὐκ ὀλίγης· ἔπειτα δὲ κᾀκ τοῦ κακοστόμαχον εἶναι τὸ ἀβρότονον, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ τὸ σέριφον, εὐστόμαχον δὲ τὸ ἀψίνθιον. ἐδείχθη γὰρ καὶ περὶ τούτων πρόσθεν ὡς τὸ μὲν πικρὸν αὐτὸ καθ’ αὑτὸ παντελῶς εἴη κακοστόμαχον, τὸ δὲ αὐστηρὸν ἢ στρυφνὸν ἢ ὅλως στῦφον εὐστόμαχον. ἐπιμιγνυμένων δὲ τῶν ποιοτήτων ἀλλήλαις ἡ σφοδροτέρα ἂν ἐπικρατοίη. ταῦτ’ οὖν ἀρκεῖ σοι γινώσκειν ἐν τῇδε τῇ πραγματείᾳ. δειχθήσεται γὰρ ἐν τοῖς τῆς θεραπευτικῆς μεθόδου γράμμασιν ὡς ἄν τις τοιούτῳ φαρμάκῳ κάλλιστα χρῷτο. καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μηκέτι ἐπιζήτει ἀκούειν μήθ’ ὅτι σὺν ἑφθῷ μήλῳ κυδονίῳ καταπλασθὲν ἢ ἄρτῳ φλεγμονὰς ὀφθαλμῶν ἰᾶται, μήθ’ ὅτι διαφορεῖ φύματα σὺν ὠμηλύσει λεῖον ἑψηθέν. οὐδὲ γὰρ τούτων οὐδέτερον οὔτε τῶν ἄλλων οὐδὲν τῆς νῦν πραγματείας ἴδιόν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς μὲν ἐμπειρικὴν διδασκαλίαν ποιουμένοις ἐν τοῖς εὐπορίστοις γράφεται φαρμάκοις, ὅσοι δὲ λογικῶς ἀσκῆσαι τὴν τέχνην βούλονται, τῆς θεραπευτικῆς ἐστι χρεία τούτοις μεθόδου. τά τε γὰρ ἄλλα καὶ βλαβείη τις ἂν μᾶλλον ἢ ὠφεληθείη πρὸς τῆς τοιαύτης ἱστορίας. Ἱπποκράτει μὲν οὖν ἐν ἀφορισμοῖς γράφοντι, ὀδύνας ὀφθαλμῶν ἀκρατοποσίη ἢ λουτρὸν ἢ πυρίη ἢ φλεβοτομίη ἢ φαρμακείη λύει· μὴ μέντοι προστιθέντι, ποίας μὲν οὖν ὀδύνας ἀκρατοποσία, ποίας δὲ λουτρὸν, καὶ τίνας μὲν πυρία, τίνας δὲ φλεβοτομία, τίνας δὲ φαρμακεία, συγχωρήσειεν ἄν τις, οἶμαι, διὰ τρεῖς αἰτίας. καὶ γὰρ ἀφοριστικὴν ἐποιεῖτο διδασκαλίαν, ἐν ᾗ διὰ τὸ σύντομον οὕτω λέγεσθαι συγκεχώρηκε τὰ πολλὰ, καὶ πάντα τὰ ἰατικὰ τῶν ὀδυνῶν ἔγραψεν, εἰ καὶ μὴ διωρίσατο πρὸς ὁποίαν ὀδύνην ποῖον αὐτῶν ἁρμόττει, ἢ καὶ πολλαχόθι τῶν ἄλλων συγγραμμάτων ἀφορμὰς ἡμῖν ἔδωκε τῶν ἐν τοῖς οὕτω ῥηθεῖσι διορισμῶν. ὅσοι δὲ μήτ’ ἐν ἑτέροις βιβλίοις ἔγραψαν ὑπὲρ τῶν τοιούτων ἀφορισμῶν μήτε ἐν διεξοδικῇ τε καὶ μακρᾷ πραγματείᾳ, γράφουσιν ἀφοριστικῶς τε καὶ βραχέως, εἴτε τὸ πρὸς τούτοις ἓν ἐκ πολλῶν δηλοῦσιν, εἰς πλείω δὲ βλάπτουσιν ἡμᾶς ἢ ὠφελοῦσι. πολλῶν γὰρ οὐσῶν διαφορῶν ἐν ταῖς ὀφθαλμίαις, καὶ μιᾶς μὲν ἐξ αὐτῶν χρῃζούσης τοῦ προειρημένου καταπλάσματος, τῶν δ’ ἄλλων βλαπτομένων, ὁ χρώμενος ἐπὶ πασῶν ἀδιορίστως πολὺ πλείους βλάψει ἢ ὠφελήσει. κατὰ τοῦτον οὖν τὸν τρόπον οὐ περὶ ἀβροτόνου μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων γραπτέον ἡμῖν ἐστι, τὰς μὲν κατὰ τὸ θερμαίνειν καὶ ψύχειν ἢ ὑγραίνειν ἢ ξηραίνειν δυνάμεις ἐξ ὧν πολλάκις εἴρηκα μεθόδων εὑρίσκουσιν, ὅσα δὲ κατὰ τὴν ἰδιότητα τῆς ὅλης οὐσίας ἀποτελοῦνται τῇ πείρᾳ μόνῃ. δέδεικται καὶ περὶ τῶν τοιούτων ὡς δηλητήριοί τέ εἰσι καὶ δηλητηρίων ἀλεξητήριοι καὶ καθαρτικοί. τούτων γὰρ οὐχ οἷόν τε λογικὴν ποιήσασθαι τὴν εὕρεσιν, ἀλλ’ ἤ μόνον ὑπόνοιάν τινα πιθανὴν ἔστιν εὑρεῖν ἐπί τινων· οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἐπὶ πάντων γε, καθάπερ καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο δεδήλωται διὰ τῶν ἔμπροσθεν. ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τῶν οὕτως εὑρισκομένων δυνάμεων ἰδίᾳ ποιήσομαι τὸν λόγον ἐν τοῖς ἐφεξῆς, ἐπειδὰν πρότερον ὑπὲρ τῶν κατὰ τὸ θερμαίνειν καὶ ψύχειν, ὑγραίνειν τε καὶ ξηραίνειν, καὶ ὅσα ταύταις ἕπονται διέλθω καθ’ ἕκαστον εἶδος φαρμάκου. τοσόνδε μέντοι προσθεὶς ἔτι περὶ ἀβροτόνου καταπαύσω τὸν λόγον, ὡς ὁ θαυμασιώτατος Πάμφιλος, καίτοι ταύτην πρώτην πόαν γράφων καὶ τάχ’ ἂν εἰ μηδενὸς τῶν ἐφεξῆς, ἀλλὰ ταύτης γοῦν ἐθελήσας αὐτόπτης γενέσθαι, ὅμως ἔσφαλται μέγιστα, νομίζων ὑπὸ Ῥωμαίων σαντόνικον ὀνομάζεσθαι τὴν βοτάνην. διαφέρει γὰρ ἀβρότονον σαντονίκου, καθότι καὶ Διοσκουρίδης ἔγραψεν ἐν τῷ τρίτῳ περὶ ὕλης ἀκριβέστατα, καὶ πάντες ἴσασι τοῦτό γε ἰατροὶ καὶ ῥωποπῶλαι. τοῦ μὲν γὰρ ἀβροτόνου δύο ἐστὶν εἴδη, τὸ μὲν ἄῤῥεν, τὸ δὲ θῆλυ νομιζόμενον, ὡς καὶ τοῦτο διώρισται παρὰ τῷ Διοσκουρίδῃ τε καὶ τῷ Παμφίλῳ καὶ ἄλλοις μυρίοις. ἕτερον δέ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ τὸ ἀψίνθιον, οὗ πάλιν εἴδη χρὴ τίθεσθαι καὶ αὐτὰ τριττὰ, ὧν τὸ μὲν τῷ γένει ὁμωνύμως προσαγορεύονται ἀψίνθιον, ὁποῖον μάλιστά ἐστι τὸ Ποντικὸν, τὸ δὲ σέριφον, τὸ δὲ σαντόνικον. εἰ δ’ ἄλλο μὲν ἀψίνθιον, ἄλλο δὲ σέριφον, ἄλλο δὲ σαντόνικον λέγοι, οὐδὲν εἰς τὰ παρόντα διαφέρει. οὐδὲ γὰρ ὄνομα διαιρήσοντες ἥκομεν, ἀλλ’ ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων σπουδάζομεν. ἐπεὶ τοίνυν καὶ ταῦτα καὶ ταῖς ἰδέαις καὶ ταῖς γεύσεσι καὶ ταῖς δυνάμεσιν ἕτερα σαφῶς ἀλλήλων ἐστὶν, ὀνομαζέτω μὲν, εἰ βούλοιτό τις, ἅπαντα διὰ μιᾶς προσηγορίας, ἐκδιδασκέτω δὲ ἀκριβῶς τὰς δυνάμεις. ἡμεῖς οὖν τὰς μὲν ἰδέας αὐτάρκως ἔφαμεν εἰρῆσθαι Διοσκουρίδῃ τε καὶ ἄλλοις οὐκ ὀλίγοις, ὥστ’ οὐ χρὴ γράφειν αὖθις ὅσα τοῖς πρόσθεν ὀρθῶς εἴρηται. εἴ τι δ’ ἐν ταῖς τούτου δυνάμεσιν ἀδιόριστον ἐκεῖνοι παρέλιπον, οὗ δὴ χάριν ἐπὶ τήνδε τὴν ἔξοδον ἀφικόμην, ἐγὼ προσθεῖναι πειράσομαι. τὸ μὲν ἀψίνθιον ἧττόν ἐστιν τῶν εἰρημένων θερμὸν, ὡς ἂν πλείστης μετέχων τῆς στύψεως. εἰ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο λεπτομερὲς ἧττον ἐκείνων, καὶ λεπτυντικὸν δὴ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἧττον ἐκείνων, οὐ μὴν ἧττόν γε ξηραντικόν. τῶν δ’ ἄλλων τὸ μὲν σαντόνικον ἀπὸ Σαντονείας χώρας, ἐν ᾗ φύεται, τὴν προσηγορίαν ἔχον ἐγγυτάτω τὴν δύναμίν ἐστι τοῦ σερίφου, βραχεῖ τινι λειπόμενον ἐν τῷ λεπτύνειν τε καὶ θερμαίνειν καὶ ξηραίνειν. αὐτὸ δὲ τὸ σέριφον ἧττον μὲν θερμὸν τοῦ ἀβροτόνου, θερμότερον δὲ ἀψινθίου, κακοστόμαχον δὲ ἱκανῶς καὶ ὡς ἂν ἁλμυρίδα τινὰ σὺν πικρότητι ἀποφαῖνον, ἔτι τε τῆς στρυφνότητος ὀλίγον μετέχον. οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἀβρότονον καὶ σαντόνικον ἱκανῶς ἐστι κακοστόμαχον. μόνον γὰρ ἐν αὐτοῖς τὸ ἀψίνθιον καὶ μάλιστα τὸ Ποντικὸν εὐστόμαχόν ἐστιν ὅτι πλείστης μετέχει στύψεως. ἀβρότονον δὲ κεκαυμένον θερμὸν καὶ ξηρόν ἐστι τὴν δύναμιν, ἔτι μᾶλλον κολοκύνθης ξηρᾶς κεκαυμένης καὶ ἀνήθου ῥίζης. ἐκεῖνα γὰρ ἕλκεσιν ὑγροῖς τε ἅμα καὶ χωρὶς φλεγμονῆς τετυλωμένοις ἁρμόττει, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μάλιστα τοῖς ἐπὶ πόσθαις αἰδοίου συμπεφωνηκέναι δοκεῖ. τοῦ δὲ ἀβροτόνου ἡ τέφρα δακνώδης ἅπασιν ἕλκεσιν ὑπάρχει. καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ πρὸς ἀλωπεκίας ἁρμόττει σὺν ἐλαίῳ λεπτομερεῖ, κικίνῳ δηλονότι ἢ ῥαφανίνῳ ἢ Σικυωνίῳ ἢ παλαιῷ, καὶ μάλιστα τῷ Σαβίνῳ. καὶ γένεια δὲ βραδέως ἀνιόντα προκαλεῖται μετά τινος τῶν εἰρημένων ἐλαίων ὅτου δὴ, καὶ οὐδὲν δ’ ἧττον ἐκείνων σχινίνῳ δευόμενον. ἀραιωτικὸν γάρ ἐστι πρὸς τῷ λεπτομερὲς εἶναι καὶ δακνῶδες καὶ θερμὸν, ἃς δὴ καὶ μάλιστα χρὴ γινώσκειν τὰς δυνάμεις αὐτοῦ καὶ μηδὲν ἔτι τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἐν τῇδε τῇ πραγματείᾳ δεῖσθαι.

6.1.1 [1. On abrotonon (southernwood) and apsinthion (wormwood) and the species of each.] Of abrotonon, this herb, there is no need to write either its form, after so many and such men, or its particular actions, as those men, even if not with distinctions, at any rate clearly set them forth. More will be said by us too about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs and in that on readily available remedies, and sometimes also in the books of the Therapeutic Method, whenever the need calls. Only, what has been set out from the beginning, to examine the general powers of all drugs, this follows in the case of the others as well, and now already it must be done and it must be stated that abrotonon is hot and dry in power, ranked somewhere in the third rank and degree of removal after the well-balanced states, having a certain dispersing and cutting power. Of the same power too is its rubbing (τρίψις), having taken it on, just as the flesh-forming and the biting. That such a rank is assessed in relation to the well-tempered nature has been said often before. And we discovered its mixture not least by judging from taste too, for it is sufficiently bitter. And such a flavour was shown to be earthy in substance, but to be thinned by abundant heat, so that it both heats and dries not ignobly. Nevertheless, also by the distinguished experience, about which much has been said before, having tested it accurately, we found this drug to be of the same mixture. For whether, having pounded the foliage together with the flowers—for the rest of it, the stalk, is useless—you sprinkle it on a clean ulcer, it appears biting and irritating; or whether, having steeped it in oil, you wish to foment either the head or the belly, it will be found to heat vigorously. And indeed those who are seized periodically by rigors, if you rub these too before the onset, they shiver less, and it does not escape the perception, immediately upon being applied, that it heats. That it is likely to kill worms, being bitter, is quite clear even before experience, if we remember what was said in the fourth of these commentaries about the nature of the bitter flavour. And you will know at once that it also has a certain dispersing and cutting power. But also that this must necessarily belong to it more than to apsinthion you will be able to reason out, first from the taste. For abrotonon partakes of some very slight acerbity, but apsinthion of not a little; and then also from the fact that abrotonon is bad for the stomach, as indeed seriphon is too, while apsinthion is good for the stomach. For it was shown about these too before that the bitter in and of itself would be entirely bad for the stomach, but the harsh or the acerbic or in general the astringent good for the stomach. And when the qualities are mixed with one another, the more vigorous would prevail. These things, then, suffice for you to know in this treatise. For it will be shown in the books of the Therapeutic Method how one might best use such a drug. And for this reason no longer seek to hear either that, applied as a plaster with boiled quince or with bread, it cures inflammations of the eyes, or that it disperses tumours (φύματα) when boiled smooth with raw barley meal. For neither of these two nor any of the others is proper to the present treatise, but for those who produce an empirical teaching it is written among the readily available drugs, whereas those who wish to practise the art rationally have need of the Therapeutic Method. For, among other things, one might be harmed rather than helped by such a history. To Hippocrates, then, writing in the Aphorisms, 'pains of the eyes drinking of unmixed wine, or a bath, or fomentation, or phlebotomy, or purging resolves', and yet not adding which pains, then, drinking of unmixed wine resolves, which a bath, and which fomentation, which phlebotomy, which purging, one would, I think, grant pardon for three reasons. For he was producing an aphoristic teaching, in which, on account of its conciseness, he has allowed many things to be said thus, and he wrote all the remedies of pains, even if he did not distinguish for which sort of pain which of them is fitting; and also in many places in his other writings he gave us starting-points for the distinctions in what was said in this way. But those who have written neither in other books about such aphorisms nor in a detailed and long treatise, write aphoristically and briefly, and if in addition to these they indicate one thing out of many, they harm us in more respects than they help. For since there are many differences among ophthalmias, and one of them needs the aforementioned plaster while the others are harmed, he who uses it in all cases without distinction will harm many more than he helps. In this manner, then, we must write not only about abrotonon but also about all the others, discovering the powers in respect of heating and cooling or moistening or drying from the methods I have often stated, but whatever is accomplished according to the peculiarity of the whole substance by experience alone. It has been shown about such things too that they are deleterious, and antidotes to deleterious things, and cathartic. For of these it is not possible to make the discovery rational, but only to find a certain plausible suspicion in some cases—not indeed in all, as this very thing too has been shown through the foregoing. But about the powers discovered in this way I shall make my discussion separately in what follows, once I have first gone through, for each species of drug, those concerning heating and cooling, moistening and drying, and whatever follows upon these. Having added, however, just so much more about abrotonon, I shall bring the discussion to an end: that the most admirable Pamphilus, although writing this herb first and perhaps, if of none of those following, at least of this one having wished to become an eyewitness, has nonetheless erred very greatly in thinking that the plant is called santonicum by the Romans. For abrotonon differs from santonicum, as Dioscorides too wrote most accurately in the third book On Materials, and all physicians and dealers in sundries know this at least. For of abrotonon there are two species, the one considered male, the other female, as this too has been distinguished in Dioscorides and Pamphilus and countless others. Different from it is apsinthion, of which again one must posit species, themselves three, of which the one is called homonymously with the genus apsinthion, of which kind the Pontic especially is, another seriphon, another santonicum. But if one should say that apsinthion is one thing, seriphon another, and santonicum another, it makes no difference for the present purposes. For we have not come to divide a name, but we are concerned about the things themselves. Since, then, these too are clearly different from one another in their forms and their tastes and their powers, let anyone, if he wishes, name them all by a single appellation, but let him teach the powers accurately. We, then, said that the forms have been sufficiently stated by Dioscorides and not a few others, so that one need not write again what has been correctly said by one's predecessors. But if those men left anything undistinguished in the powers of this plant, for the sake of which indeed I have come to this digression, I shall try to add it. Apsinthion is less hot than those mentioned, as partaking of the most astringency. And if this too is less fine-particled than they, it is also thinning, in the same manner, less than they, yet not indeed less drying. Of the others, santonicum, having its name from the Santonian country in which it grows, is nearest in power to seriphon, falling short by some little in thinning and heating and drying. Seriphon itself is less hot than abrotonon, but hotter than apsinthion, sufficiently bad for the stomach and as displaying a certain saltiness together with bitterness, and further partaking of a little acerbity. So too abrotonon and santonicum are sufficiently bad for the stomach. For alone among them apsinthion, and especially the Pontic, is good for the stomach, because it partakes of the most astringency. Burnt abrotonon is hot and dry in power, still more than burnt dry gourd and root of dill. For those are fitting for ulcers that are moist and at the same time callused without inflammation, and for this reason especially they seem to agree with those on the foreskins of the genitals. But the ash of abrotonon is biting to all ulcers. And for this reason it is fitting also against alopecia with fine-particled oil, namely castor-oil or radish-oil or Sicyonian or old oil, and especially Sabine. And it brings forth beards that come up slowly with whichever of the oils mentioned, and no less than those when moistened with mastic-oil. For it is rarefying, in addition to being fine-particled and biting and hot, which powers of it indeed one must especially know, and no longer need anything of the particulars in this treatise.

6.1.1 [1. On southernwood and wormwood and the species of each.] Of southernwood, this herb, one need not describe the form, after so many men of such quality, nor its particular actions, since those men set them out, if not with precise distinctions, at least clearly. More will also be said by us about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs and in that on easily procured remedies, and sometimes also in the writings of the Therapeutic Method, when need calls. Only what was proposed from the beginning, to examine the universal powers of all drugs, follows in the case of the others too, and it must now already be done here. It must be said that southernwood is hot and dry in power, ranked somewhere in the third order and remove beyond the balanced state, and has a certain dispersing and cutting power. Of the same power also is its rubbing (?) having taken [it] (τρίψις … εἰληφυῖα), as also the flesh-forming and the biting. That such an order is assessed relative to the well-tempered nature has often been said before. We found out its mixture not least by judging also from taste, for it is quite bitter. Such a flavour was shown to be earthy in its substance and to be thinned by abundant heat, so as both to heat and to dry not feebly. Moreover, having tested it accurately also by the qualified experience, about which it has often been said before, we found this drug to be of the same mixture. For if you pound the foliage together with the flowers (for the rest of it, the dry stalk, is useless) and sprinkle it on a clean ulcer, it appears biting and irritant; and if you steep it in oil and choose to pour it over either the head or the belly, it will be found to heat strongly. And indeed those who are seized by rigors at periods, if you rub them down with it before the onset, shiver less; nor does it escape perception, immediately as it is applied, that it heats. That it is likely to destroy worms, being bitter, is clear even before experience, if we remember anything of what was said in the fourth of these commentaries about the nature of the bitter flavour. You will know at once that it also has a certain dispersing and cutting power. And that this must belong to it more than to wormwood you will be able to infer, first from the taste. For southernwood partakes of a very small acerbity, but wormwood of not a little; and then also from the fact that southernwood is bad for the stomach, as is seriphon too, whereas wormwood is good for the stomach. For it was shown earlier about these things too that the bitter by itself is wholly bad for the stomach, whereas the harsh or acerbic or, in general, the astringent is good for the stomach; and when the qualities are mixed with one another, the stronger would prevail. This, then, is enough for you to know in this treatise. For it will be shown in the writings of the Therapeutic Method how one may best use such a drug. And for this reason do not seek any longer to hear either that, applied as a poultice with boiled quince or with bread, it heals inflammations of the eyes, or that, boiled smooth with ōmēlysis, it disperses phymata. For neither of these nor any of the others is proper to the present treatise; rather, for those who give an empirical teaching it is written in the easily procured drugs, while those who wish to practise the art rationally have need of the Therapeutic Method. For, among other things, one would be harmed rather than benefited by such a report. Now Hippocrates, writing in the Aphorisms, 'pains of the eyes are resolved by drinking of unmixed wine, or a bath, or a vapour-bath, or venesection, or purging', yet not adding what kind of pains drinking of unmixed wine resolves, what kind a bath, which a vapour-bath, which venesection, which purging, one would pardon, I think, for three reasons. For he was giving an aphoristic teaching, in which, because of brevity, many things are allowed to be stated in this way; and he wrote down all the remedies of the pains, even if he did not distinguish which of them suits which kind of pain; or else in many places of his other writings he has given us starting-points for the distinctions in what was stated in this way. But those who have written about such aphorisms neither in other books nor in a detailed and long treatise, but write aphoristically and briefly, and besides this (εἴτε τὸ πρὸς τούτοις) indicate one thing out of many, harm us in more cases than they help. For since there are many differentiae among ophthalmias, and one of them requires the aforementioned poultice while the others are harmed by it, he who uses it on all of them without distinction will harm many more than he helps. In this manner, then, we must write not about southernwood alone but about all the others as well, the powers relating to heating and cooling or moistening or drying being found (εὑρίσκουσιν) by the methods I have often spoken of, but whatever is effected by the peculiarity of the whole substance by experience alone. It has been shown about such things too that they are deleterious, and protective against deleterious things, and purgative. For of these it is not possible to make a rational discovery; rather, it is only possible to find in some cases a certain plausible conjecture, and not indeed in all, just as this very point has been made clear in what precedes. But about the powers found in this way I shall give an account separately in what follows, once I have first gone through, for each species of drug, what concerns heating and cooling, moistening and drying, and whatever follows on these. Having added this much more about southernwood, however, I shall end the discussion: that the most admirable Pamphilus, although writing of this as his first herb, and having perhaps wished, if of none of the following, at least of this one to become an eyewitness, nevertheless erred most greatly, believing that the plant is called santonicum by the Romans. For southernwood differs from santonicum, as Dioscorides too wrote most accurately in the third book On Materials, and all physicians and dealers in small wares (ῥωποπῶλαι) know this at least. For of southernwood there are two species, one considered male, the other female, as this too has been distinguished by Dioscorides and Pamphilus and countless others. Different from it is wormwood, of which again one must posit species, and these threefold: of which one is called wormwood, homonymously with the genus, of which kind especially is the Pontic, another seriphon, another santonicum. But if one should say that wormwood is one thing, seriphon another, and santonicum another, it makes no difference for present purposes. For we have not come to divide a name, but are concerned with the things themselves. Since, then, these are clearly different from one another in form, in taste and in powers, let anyone, if he wishes, name them all by a single appellation, but let him teach their powers accurately. We said, then, that the forms have been described adequately by Dioscorides and not a few others, so that one need not write again what was correctly said by our predecessors. But if those men left anything undistinguished in the powers of this one, for the sake of which indeed I have come to this exposition (ἔξοδον), I shall try to add it. Wormwood is less hot than those mentioned, inasmuch as it partakes of the most astringency. And if it is also less fine-particled than those, it is then in the same way also less thinning than those, yet not less drying. Of the others, santonicum, which has its appellation from the Santonian country in which it grows, is nearest in power to seriphon, falling short by a little in thinning, heating and drying. Seriphon itself is less hot than southernwood but hotter than wormwood, and quite bad for the stomach, as presenting a certain saltiness together with bitterness, and it further partakes a little of acerbity. So too southernwood and santonicum are quite bad for the stomach. For among them wormwood alone, and especially the Pontic, is good for the stomach, because it partakes of the most astringency. Burnt southernwood is hot and dry in power, even more so than burnt dry gourd and dill root. For those suit ulcers that are moist and at the same time calloused without inflammation, and for this reason they seem to be especially in accord with those on the prepuce of the genitals. But the ash of southernwood is biting to all ulcers. And for this reason it suits alopeciae, with a fine-particled oil, namely castor oil or radish oil or Sicyonian or old oil, and especially the Sabine. It also calls forth beards that are slow to come up, with any one of the oils mentioned, and no less than with those when moistened with mastic oil. For it is rarefying, besides being fine-particled, biting and hot; and these are the powers of it that one must especially know, and needs nothing further of the particulars in this treatise.

6.1.2 [β΄. Περὶ ἄγνου ἢ λύγου.] Ἄγνος δὲ ἢ λύγος, τὸ θαμνῶδες φυτὸν, θερμὸς μέν ἐστι καὶ ξηραντικὸς κατὰ τὴν τρίτην που ἀπόστασιν, λεπτομερὴς δὲ ἱκανῶς καὶ γευόμενος δριμύς τε ἅμα καὶ στύφων ἄγνος, ἢ λύγος. αὐτὰς μὲν δὴ τὰς λύγους ἀχρήστους ἔχει πρὸς ἰατρείαν, τὰ δὲ φύλλα καὶ τὸ σπέρμα ξηρὰ καὶ θερμὰ τὴν δύναμίν ἐστι καὶ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν λεπτομερῆ. καὶ γὰρ χρωμένων οὕτω φαίνεται καὶ γευομένων δριμύ τε ἅμα καὶ ὑποστῦφόν ἐστι καὶ τὸ φύλλον καὶ τὸ ἄνθος καὶ ὁ καρπός. ἔστι δὲ καὶ ἐδώδιμος ὁ καρπὸς καὶ θερμαίνει σαφῶς μετὰ τοῦ κεφαλαλγὴς ὑπάρχειν. εἰ δὲ φρυχθείη, καὶ γὰρ καὶ οὕτως ἐσθίεται μετὰ τραγημάτων, ἧττον ἅπτεται τῆς κεφαλῆς. ἄφυσος δὲ κατὰ γαστέρα καὶ ὁ ἄφρυκτος μὲν, ἐπὶ μᾶλλον δὲ πεφρυγμένος. ἐπέχει δὲ καὶ τὰς πρὸς ἀφροδίσια ὁρμὰς ὅ τε πεφρυγμένος καὶ ὁ ἄφρυκτος καρπὸς, καὶ τὰ φύλλα καὶ τὰ ἄνθη τοῦ θάμνου ταὐτὸ τοῦτο δύναται δρᾷν, ὥστε οὐ μόνον ἐσθιόμενα καὶ πινόμενα πρὸς ἁγνείαν πεπίστευται συντελεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑποστρωννύμενα. ταῦτ’ ἄρα καὶ τοῖς Θεσμοφορίοις αἱ γυναῖκες Ἀθήνῃσιν ὑποστρωννύουσιν ἑαυταῖς ὅλον τὸν θάμνον, ἐντεῦθεν δὲ καὶ τοὔνομα αὐτῷ. ἐξ ὧν ἁπάντων δῆλον, εἴ γε τῶν ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ὑπομνήμασιν εἰρημένων μεμνήμεθα, θερμαίνειν τε ἅμα καὶ ξηραίνειν καὶ ἀφυσότατον ὑπάρχειν ἄγνον. ὅτι δὲ λεπτομερὴς ἀκριβῶς ἐστιν ἡ δύναμις αὐτοῦ τεκμήριον. καὶ γὰρ τὸ πρὸς κεφαλὴν. ἅπτειν οὐ διὰ πλῆθος ἀτμώδους πνεύματος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γεννωμένου μᾶλλον ἤπερ διὰ θερμότητα καὶ λεπτομέρειαν εὔλογον γίνεται. εἴ περ γὰρ ἦν φυσώδους πνεύματος γεννητικὸν, ἐνεφύσησέ τε ἂν τὴν γαστέρα καὶ τὰς πρὸς ἀφροδίσια παρώξυνεν ὁρμὰς ὥσπερ εὔζωμον. ἐπεὶ δὲ οὐ μόνον οὐ παροξύνει, ἀλλὰ καὶ καταστέλλειν πέφυκεν, εἴη ἂν κατὰ τὴν πηγάνου μάλιστα δύναμιν ἐν τῷ θερμαίνειν καὶ ξηραίνειν, οὐ μὴν ἶσόν γ’ ἐστὶν αὐτῷ. βραχὺ γὰρ ἀπολείπεται κατ’ ἄμφω· καὶ γὰρ θερμαντικώτερον αὐτοῦ καὶ ξηραντικώτερόν ἐστι τὸ πήγανον. διενήνοχε δὲ καὶ τῷ τῆς ποιότητος καὶ δυνάμεως ἐπιμίκτῳ. τὸ γὰρ τοῦ ἄγνου σπέρμα καὶ οἱ βλαστοὶ στύψιν τινὰ μετρίαν ἐπεισφέρουσι. τὸ δὲ πήγανον ὅταν μὲν ξηρὸν ᾖ, πικρὸν ἀκριβῶς ἐστι καὶ δριμὺ, ὅταν δὲ ὑγρὸν, ὑπόπικρον. οὐ μὴν αὐστηρόν γε ἢ στρυφνόν τι πρόσεστιν αὐτῷ, ἢ εἰ καὶ προσεῖναί τῳ δόξειεν, ἀμυδρὸν παντάπασιν οἶδ’ ὅτι δόξει, καὶ οὐδαμῶς ἶσον τῷ τοῦ ἄγνου. ταῦτ’ ἄρα καὶ πρὸς ἧπαρ καὶ σπλῆνα σκληρούμενά τε καὶ ἐμφραττόμενα τὸ τοῦ ἄγνου σπέρμα μᾶλλον ἢ πήγανον ἁρμόττει. τῆς θεραπευτικῆς δέ ἐστιν ἤδη ταῦτα μεθόδου, ἧς τὸ μὲν μηδ’ ὅλως προσάπτεσθαι φαρμάκων 6.1.2 [2. On agnos or lygos.] Agnos or lygos, the shrubby plant, is hot and drying at about the third degree of departure, fine-particled to a considerable extent, and to the taste pungent and at the same time astringent — agnos, or lygos. The withies (lygoi) themselves which it bears are useless for medicine, but the leaves and the seed are dry and hot in power and fine-particled in substance. For so it appears to those who use it, and to those who taste it the leaf, the flower and the fruit are at once pungent and somewhat astringent. The fruit is also edible, and it heats manifestly, besides being productive of headache. If it is roasted — for it is eaten in this way too among the dessert-nuts — it affects the head less. It is non-flatulent in the belly, both the unroasted and, still more, the roasted. Both the roasted and the unroasted fruit also check the impulses toward sexual intercourse, and the leaves and flowers of the shrub are able to do this same thing, so that not only when eaten and drunk are they believed to contribute to chastity, but also when strewn beneath. For this reason, too, at the Thesmophoria the women at Athens strew the whole shrub beneath themselves, and from this comes its name. From all this it is clear, if we remember what was said in the preceding commentaries, that agnos heats and at the same time dries and is most non-flatulent. And there is a proof that its power is precisely fine-particled: for its affecting the head comes about, on good reasoning, not through an abundance of vaporous pneuma generated by it, but rather through heat and fineness of particles. For if it were generative of flatulent pneuma, it would have inflated the belly and would have sharpened the impulses toward sexual intercourse, like rocket. But since it not only does not sharpen them but is by nature apt to suppress them, it would be most of all of the power of rue in heating and drying; yet it is not equal to it. For it falls short a little in both; for rue is both more heating and more drying than it. It differs also in the admixture of quality and power. For the seed of agnos and the shoots bring in a certain moderate astringency, whereas rue, when it is dry, is precisely bitter and pungent, and when moist, slightly bitter. Yet nothing harsh or acerbic is attached to it, or if it should seem to someone to be attached, I know it will seem altogether faint, and in no way equal to that of agnos. For this reason, too, the seed of agnos is more suitable than rue for liver and spleen when they are hardened and obstructed. But these matters already belong to the therapeutic method, from which to refrain altogether while pronouncing on the power of drugs is impossible, whereas to leave it quickly and return again to what is set before us would be the work of a prudent man. Still more in the case of the drugs that follow I shall try to do just this, I mean to reckon out the general power from some few evident facts and then withdraw from the particular actions. For it suffices for the present purposes to know only this, that agnos is hot and dry in power, not moderately but at about the third of the degrees of departure, and fine-particled to a considerable extent. For he who knows these things, and then learns in addition the therapeutic method, will himself discover how he will move the menses by means of it, how he will disperse hardened parts, and how he will prepare by means of it an anointment against fatigue or a heating one.

That its power is precisely fine-particled, there is evidence. For if it were productive of windy pneuma, it would both have inflated the belly and have roused the impulses towards sexual intercourse, as rocket does. But these matters already belong to the therapeutic method: it is impossible, when declaring the power of drugs, not to touch upon it at all, but to leave it quickly and return again to the matter proposed would be the work of a sensible man. Still more in the case of the drugs that follow I shall try to do this very thing, I mean, having inferred the general power from a few evident facts, to withdraw from the particular activities. 6.1.3 [γ΄. Περὶ ἀγρώστεως.] Τῆς δὲ ἀγρώστεως ἡ μὲν ῥίζα συμμέτρως ἐστὶ ψυχρὰ καὶ ξηρὰ, ἔχουσά τι ὀλίγον δακνῶδες καὶ λεπτομερές. ἡ δὲ πόα ψύχει μὲν κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ἀπόστασιν, σύμμετρος δ’ ἐστὶ κατὰ ὑγρότητα καὶ ξηρότητα. τὸ δὲ σπέρμα τῆς μὲν ἄλλης ἀσθενὲς ὑπάρχει, τῆς δ’ ἐν τῷ Παρνασσῷ ξηραντικόν τε καὶ λεπτομερὲς καὶ ὑπόστρυφνον. ἄγρωστις ἐδώδιμον ἔχει τὴν ῥίζαν, ἔστ’ ἂν ᾖ μαλακὴ, γλυκεῖα μὲν ὑδατώδης, δριμὺ δέ τι καὶ ὑπόστρυφνον ὀλίγον ἔχουσα. αὕτη δὲ ἡ πόα τελέως ἐστὶν ὑδατώδης γευομένοις. ἐξ ὧν δῆλον ὡς μετρίως μέν ἐστιν ἡ ῥίζα ψυχρὰ καὶ ξηρὰ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο κολλητικὸν τῶν ἐναίμων ἑλκῶν. αὐτὴ δὲ ἡ πόα καταπλασσομένη ψύχει μὲν οὐκ ἰσχυρῶς, ὑγρότητος δὲ καὶ ξηρότητος ἐν τῷ μέσῳ καθέστηκε. τὸ δὲ ἐν τῇ ῥίζῃ δακνῶδες καὶ λεπτομερές ἐστι μὲν ὀλίγον, εἴωθε δ’ οὖν ἔστιν ὅτε καὶ λίθους θρύπτειν, εἴ τις αὐτὴν ἀφεψήσας πίνοι. τὸ δὲ σπέρμα τῆς μὲν ἄλλης ἀσθενές ἐστιν, τῆς δ’ ἐν τῷ Παρνασσῷ διουρητικόν τέ ἐστι καὶ ῥεύματα ξηραίνει γαστρὸς καὶ στομάχου. δύναμις γάρ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ξηραντική τε καὶ λεπτομερὴς καὶ ὑπόστρυφνος.

6.1.3 [3. On agrostis.] Of agrostis the root is moderately cold and dry, having something slightly biting and fine-particled. The herb itself cools in the first degree of distance, but is balanced in respect of moisture and dryness. The seed of the other kind is weak, but that of the kind on Parnassus is drying, fine-particled and somewhat astringent. Agrostis has an edible root, so long as it is soft, sweet and watery, yet having something pungent and a little that is somewhat astringent. The herb itself is entirely watery to those who taste it. From which it is clear that the root is moderately cold and dry, and for this reason agglutinating of bleeding wounds. The herb itself, applied as a plaster, cools, though not strongly, and stands in the middle between moisture and dryness. The biting and fine-particled element in the root is indeed small, yet it is nonetheless wont at times even to break up stones, if one boils it down and drinks it. The seed of the other kind is weak, but that of the kind on Parnassus is diuretic and dries fluxes of the belly and of the stomach. For its power is drying, fine-particled and somewhat astringent.

6.1.4 [4. On anchousa and the four kinds of anchousa.] Of anchousa there is a fourth kind (τέταρτόν ἐστιν εἶδος; the sense intended is that there are four species), of which the onokleia has a root that cools considerably and dries, being at once astringent and slightly bitter, and capable also of thinning and scouring away the bilious humours and of condensing the bodies. Its leaves it has weaker than the root, yet they too are astringent and dry. And the one called lykopsis cools and dries, and has a root more astringent than that of the onokleia. The onocheilos is both hotter and more drug-like; for it has more of the pungent, and that immediately to the taste. Hotter still than this is the one which is small and more bitter and happens to be still more drug-like. The anchousai, then, are not all of the same power. For the one called onokleia has a root at once astringent and slightly bitter, capable both of condensing the bodies and of moderately thinning and scouring away and washing off the bilious and salty humours. For it was said in what precedes that the acerbic quality, when mixed with the bitter, is by nature such as to produce these effects. Thus indeed it is also beneficial to those suffering from jaundice, from the spleen and from the kidneys. It is also capable of cooling, and when applied as a plaster with barley-meal it helps erysipelas; and it scours not only when drunk but also when applied externally, and for this reason it cures alphos and lepra with vinegar. These are the works of the root, and the powers behind the works are those stated. The leaves of the plant are weaker than the root, but are not free of drying and of being astringent, so that they also cure diarrhoea when drunk with wine. And the one called lykopsis is likewise suited to cases of erysipelas and has a root more astringent than that of the onokleia. Of the onocheilos, also called Alcibiadeion, the power is more drug-like; at any rate it has more of the pungent, and that immediately to the taste, and it is quite suitable for those bitten by vipers, applied as a plaster, worn as an amulet, and eaten. The remaining fourth one, small and alone among them almost nameless, is similar to the Alcibiadeion, but is more bitter and still more drug-like, and for this reason is suited against the broad worms, drunk in the quantity of an oxybaphon with hyssop and cress.

Of these, onokleia has a root that cools and dries considerably, and is at once astringent and somewhat bitter, able to thin and to cleanse away the bilious humours and to condense bodies. Its leaves are weaker than the root, but they too are astringent and drying. The one called lykopsis also cools and dries, but has a root more astringent than that of onokleia. Onocheilos is hotter and more drug-like, for it has more of the pungent, which is evident to the taste at once. Hotter still than this is the one that is small, more bitter and more drug-like still. The anchousai are not all of the same power. The one called onokleia has a root at once astringent and somewhat bitter, able to condense bodies and moderately to thin, cleanse away and wash out the bilious and salty humours. For it was said earlier that the acerbic quality, mixed with the bitter, naturally produces these effects. In this way it is beneficial to those with jaundice, to splenetics and to nephritics. It is also able to cool, and applied as a poultice with barley-groats it helps erysipelas. It cleanses not only when drunk but also when applied externally, and for this reason it heals alphoi and leprai with vinegar. These are the effects of the root, and the powers behind those effects are those stated. The leaves of the plant are weaker than the root, but they are not without drying and astringency, so that, drunk with wine, they also heal diarrhoea. The one called lykopsis is likewise suited to cases of erysipelas, and has a root more astringent than that of onokleia. The power of onocheilos, also called Alkibiadeios, is more drug-like. At any rate it has more of the pungent, evident to the taste at once, and it is well suited to people bitten by vipers, whether applied as a poultice, hung on as an amulet or eaten. The remaining fourth, which is small and almost alone among them without a name, is close to the Alkibiadeios, but more bitter and still more drug-like. For this reason it is useful against flat worms, drunk in the quantity of an oxybaphon with hyssop and cress.

Περὶ ῥίζης ἀγαρικοῦ.] Ἀγαρικοῦ ῥίζα τοῦτ’ ἔστιν ἐπιφυομένη πρέμνῳ, κατὰ μὲν τὴν πρώτην γεῦσιν γλυκεῖά τις, ὑπόπικρος δὲ ὀλίγον ὕστερον φαινομένη καί τινος ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ δριμύτητος ἔμφασιν ἐπάγουσα, καὶ βραχείας στύψεως. ἔστι δὲ καὶ χαύνη τὴν σύστασιν. ἐξ ὧν ἁπάντων εὔδηλον, εἴπερ τῶν ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ὑπομνήμασιν εἰρημένων μνημονεύομεν, ὡς σύνθετόν ἐστι τὸ φάρμακον ἐξ οὐσίας ἀερώδους τε καὶ γεώδους, ὑπὸ θερμότητος λελεπτυσμένης, ἥκιστα δὲ τῆς ὑδατώδους μετέχει. ταῦτ’ ἄρα διαφορητικήν τε καὶ θερμαντικὴν τὴν δύναμιν ἔχει, καὶ πάχους τμητικὴν καὶ διακαθαίρει τὰς ἐν τοῖς σπλάγχνοις ἐμφράξεις, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἰκτεριῶντας ἰᾶται, τοὺς ἐπ’ ἐμφράξει τῶν καθ’ ἧπαρ οὕτω κάμνοντας. ὀνίνησι δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἐπιλήπτους διὰ τὴν αὐτὴν δύναμιν καὶ ῥίγη τὰ κατὰ περίοδον, ὅσα παχέων ἢ γλίσχρων ἐστὶ χυλῶν ἔγγονα, καὶ ταῦτα ἰᾶται. ὠφελεῖ δὲ καὶ τοὺς ὑπὸ κατὰ ψύξιν ἀδικούντων θηρίων δηχθέντας, ἢ νυγέντας, ἔξωθέν τε κατὰ τοῦ πεπονθότος ἐπιτιθέμενον, εἴσω τε τοῦ σώματος λαμβάνον ὁλκῇ δραχμῆς μιᾶς μετ’ οἴνου κεκραμένου. ἔστι δὲ καὶ καθαρτικόν.

6.1.5 [5. On the root of agaric.] Agaric is a root, that is to say, one growing upon a trunk; at the first taste it is somewhat sweet, but a little later it shows itself slightly bitter, and in time it brings on the impression of a certain pungency, and of a slight astringency. It is also loose in consistency. From all of which it is quite clear, if indeed we remember what was said in the earlier commentaries, that the drug is composed of an airy and an earthy substance, thinned by heat, and that it participates least of all in the watery. For these reasons, then, it has a dispersing and heating power, and one cutting of thickness, and it cleanses out the obstructions in the viscera, and on this account heals those suffering from jaundice, those who are so afflicted because of an obstruction of the parts in the region of the liver. It benefits epileptics too through the same power, and periodic rigors, such as are the offspring of thick or viscous juices—these also it heals. It also helps those bitten or stung by beasts that do harm by chilling, both applied externally over the affected part and taken into the body in a weight of one drachm with diluted wine. It is also purgative.

6.1.5 [5. On the root of agaric.] The root of agaric, that is, the growth upon a tree-trunk, appears at the first taste somewhat sweet, but a little later somewhat bitter, and in time it brings on an impression of a certain pungency and of slight astringency. It is also loose in its consistency. From all of this it is quite clear, if we remember what was said in the preceding treatises, that the drug is compounded of an airy and earthy substance thinned by heat, and has very little share in the watery substance. It therefore has a dispersing and heating power, and one that is cutting of thickness; it clears out the obstructions in the viscera, and for this reason it heals those suffering from jaundice, that is, those who are ill in this way from obstruction of the parts about the liver. By the same power it also benefits epileptics, and it heals periodic rigors as well, those that are the offspring of thick or viscid juices. It also helps those bitten or stung by wild creatures that do harm by chilling, both when it is applied externally on the affected part and when it is taken into the body in the weight of one drachm with mixed wine. It is also purgative.

Περὶ ἀκακίας.] Ἀκακίας καὶ τὸ φυτὸν μὲν αὐτὸ στρυφνόν ἐστι, καὶ ὁ καρπὸς καὶ ὁ χυλὸς, ὅστις καὶ πλυθεὶς ἀσθενέστερός τε ἅμα καὶ ἀδηκτότερος γίγνεται, ὥς τινα δριμύτητα κατὰ τὴν πλύσιν ἀποτιθέμενος. εἰ δὴ καὶ ἐπαλειφθείη κατά τινος ὑγιοῦς μέρους, εὐθὺς τοῦτο ξηρότερόν τε καὶ συντεταμένον ἀποφαίνει, καὶ θερμασίας μὲν αἴσθησιν οὐδέποτε, ψύξιν δὲ οὐκ ἄγαν ἰσχυρὰν ἔχει. δῆλον οὖν ὅτι ψυχρόν τε καὶ γεῶδές ἐστι τὸ φάρμακον, ἀναμεμιγμένης αὐτῷ τινος καὶ ὑδατώδους οὐσίας. εἰκασθείη δ’ ἂν οὐδ’ ὁμοιομερὲς ὑπάρχειν, ἀλλ’ ἔχειν τινὰ μόρια διεσπαρμένα καὶ λεπτομερῆ καὶ θερμὰ, κατὰ τὴν πλύσιν ἀποχωροῦντα. καὶ κείσθω καὶ τοῦτο τῆς τρίτης μὲν τάξεως τῶν ξηραινόντων, τῆς δευτέρας δὲ τῶν ψυχόντων, ἐπειδὰν πλυθῇ, τὸ δὲ ἄπλυτον τῆς πρώτης.

6.1.12 [12. On akakia (acacia).] Of akakia both the plant itself is acerbic, and its fruit and its juice, which, when it has also been washed, becomes at once both weaker and less biting, as though laying aside a certain pungency in the washing. If, indeed, it is smeared on some healthy part, it at once renders this drier and contracted, and it never produces a sensation of heat, but has a cooling that is not very strong. It is clear, then, that the drug is cold and earthy, with a certain watery substance also mixed in with it. One might conjecture, too, that it is not homoeomerous, but has certain scattered parts that are fine-particled and hot, which depart in the washing. And let this too be placed in the third order of drying agents, and in the second of cooling agents, when it has been washed; the unwashed, however, in the first.

6.1.12 [12. On acacia.] Of acacia, both the plant itself is acerbic, and so are the fruit and the juice; the juice, when washed, becomes at the same time weaker and less biting, as though it laid aside some pungency in the washing. And if it is smeared on some healthy part, it at once renders this drier and drawn tight, and it never produces any sensation of heating, but a cooling that is not very strong. It is clear, then, that the drug is cold and earthy, with some watery substance also mixed into it. One might conjecture that it is not even uniform in its parts, but has certain particles dispersed through it that are fine-particled and hot, and that these depart in the washing. And let this drug too be placed in the third order of drying things and in the second of cooling things once it has been washed, and the unwashed in the first.

Περὶ ἀκαλύφης.] Ἀκαλύφη. καὶ ταύτης τῆς πόας ὅ τε καρπὸς καὶ τὰ φύλλα, ταῦτα γὰρ καὶ εἰς χρεῖαν ἥκει μάλιστα, διαφορητικῆς ἱκανῶς ἐστι δυνάμεως, ὥστε καὶ φύματα καὶ παρωτίδας ἰᾶται. ἔχει δέ τι καὶ φυσῶδες, ᾧ καὶ πρὸς τὰς συνουσίας ὁρμὰς ἐπεγείρει, καὶ μάλισθ’ ὅταν μετὰ γλυκέος πίνηται τὸ σπέρμα. ὅτι δ’ οὐ θερμαίνει μὲν σφοδρῶς, λεπτομερὲς δὲ ἱκανῶς ἐστιν, ἥ τε τῶν ἐν θώρακί τε καὶ πνεύμονι παχέων καὶ γλίσχρων χυμῶν ἀναγωγὴ μαρτυρεῖ καὶ τὸ κνεῖσθαι τὰ μόρια τοῦ σώματος ὧν προσψαύσῃ. τὸ δὲ πνευματῶδες, οὗ μετέχειν εἴρηται, πεττομένης αὐτῆς γεννᾶται. οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἐνεργείᾳ πνευματῶδες, ἀλλὰ δυνάμει. κοιλίαν δὲ ὑπάγει μετρίως αὐτῷ μόνῳ τῷ ῥύπτειν καὶ οἷον γαργαλίζειν, οὐ τῷ καθαίρειν. καὶ τὰ γαγγραινώδη καὶ τὰ καρκινώδη καὶ ὅλως ὅσα ξηρανθῆναι δεῖται χωρὶς τοῦ δάκνεσθαι προσηκόντως ἰᾶται, λεπτομερὴς μὲν ὑπάρχουσα καὶ ξηρὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν, οὐ μὴν εἰς τοσοῦτόν γε μετέχουσα θερμότητος ὡς ἤδη δάκνειν.

6.1.13 [13. On akalyphe.] Akalyphe. Of this herb too, both the fruit and the leaves—for it is these especially that come into use—are of a sufficiently dispersing power, so that it heals both phymata and parotid swellings. It also has something flatulent in it, by which it also arouses the impulses toward sexual intercourse, and especially when the seed is drunk with sweet wine. That it does not heat violently, but is sufficiently fine-particled, is attested both by the bringing-up of the thick and viscous humours in the chest and lung, and by the fact that the parts of the body which it touches itch. But the pneumatic quality, in which it has been said to share, is generated as it is being digested; for it is not pneumatic in actuality, but in potentiality. It moves the bowels moderately by the mere fact of cleansing and, as it were, tickling, not by purging. And gangrenous and cancerous conditions, and in general whatever needs to be dried without being bitten, it heals appropriately, being fine-particled and dry in its mixture, yet not sharing in heat to such a degree as actually to bite.

6.1.13 [13. On nettle.] Nettle. Of this herb too both the fruit and the leaves (for it is these that chiefly come into use) are of a sufficiently dispersing power, so that they heal both phymata and parotid swellings. It also has something flatulent, by which it also stirs up urges to sexual intercourse, and especially when the seed is drunk with sweet wine. That it does not heat strongly, but is sufficiently fine-particled, is attested both by the bringing up of the thick and viscous humours in the thorax and lung and by the itching of those parts of the body which it touches. The windy quality, in which it has been said to share, is generated when it is digested; for it is not windy in actuality, but in potentiality. It moves the bowel moderately solely by cleansing and, as it were, tickling, not by purging. And it fittingly heals gangrenous and cancerous lesions and in general whatever needs to be dried without being bitten, being fine-particled and dry in its mixture, yet not sharing in heat to such a degree as already to bite.

6.1.23 [κγ΄. Περὶ ἀλόης.] Ἀλόη. αὕτη μὲν ἡ πόα παρ’ ἡμῖν οὐ πάνυ τι φύεται, καὶ ἡ φυομένη δὲ κατὰ Συρίαν τὴν μεγάλην ὑδατωδεστέρα τε καὶ ἀσθενεστέρα τὴν δύναμίν ἐστιν. ἄχρι μέντοι τοσούτου ξηραίνειν πέφυκεν ὡς κολλᾷν τραύματα. κατὰ δὲ τὰς θερμοτέρας χώρας, ὧν ἐστιν ἡ κοίλη Συρία καὶ Ἀραβία, πολὺ βελτίων ἐστίν. ἀρίστη δὲ καὶ ἡ κατὰ τὴν Ἰνδίαν, ἧς ὀπός ἐστιν τὸ κομιζόμενον ἐνταυθοῖ τοῦτο φάρμακον ἡ ἀλόη προσαγορευομένη, χρείαν παμπόλλην παρεχόμενον ἐκ τοῦ ξηραίνειν ἀδήκτως. ἔστι δὲ οὐχ ἁπλῆς φύσεως, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ καὶ ἡ γεῦσις μαρτυρεῖ, στύφει τε ἅμα καὶ πικράζει. στύφει μὲν οὖν μετρίως, πικρὰ δὲ ἰσχυρῶς ἐστιν. ὑπάγει δὲ καὶ γαστέρα τῶν ἐκκοπρωτικῶν καλουμένων οὖσα φαρμάκων, ὥστε ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων δῆλον, εἴ τι μεμνήμεθα τῶν ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ λόγῳ δεδειγμένων, ὡς τῶν μὲν ξηραινόντων φαρμάκων τῆς τρίτης ἐστὶν ἀποστάσεως, τῶν θερμαινόντων δὲ ἤτοι τῆς πρώτης ἐπιτεταμένης ἢ τῆς δευτέρας ἐκλελυμένης. τῷ δὲ μικτῷ τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῆς μαρτυρεῖ καὶ τὰ κατὰ μέρος ἔργα. καὶ γὰρ εὐστόμαχόν ἐστι τὸ φάρμακον, εἴπέρ τι καὶ ἄλλο, καὶ κόλπων κολλητικόν. ἰᾶται δὲ τὰ δυσεπούλωτα τῶν ἑλκῶν, καὶ μάλιστα τὰ καθ’ ἕδραν τε καὶ αἰδοῖον. ὠφελεῖ δὲ καὶ τὰς φλεγμονὰς αὐτῶν ὕδατι διεθεῖσα καὶ κολλᾷ τραύματα κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον. ἁρμόζει δὲ ὡσαύτως χρωμένῳ καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐν στόματι καὶ ῥισὶ καὶ ὀφθαλμοῖς φλεγμονάς. καὶ ὅλως ἀποκρούεσθαί τε καὶ διαφορεῖν ἅμα πέφυκεν, μετὰ καὶ τοῦ ῥύπτειν ἐπ’ ὀλίγον, εἰς ὅσον ἕλκεσι καθαροῖς ἄλυπον.

6.1.23 [23. On aloe.] Aloe. This herb does not grow much at all in our country, and that which grows in Greater Syria is more watery and weaker in its power. Nevertheless it is of such a nature as to dry to the extent of agglutinating wounds. But in the hotter regions, among which are Coele Syria and Arabia, it is much better. Best of all, too, is that in India, whose juice is this drug that is imported here, called aloe, which furnishes very great usefulness through drying without biting. It is not of a simple nature, but, as the taste also bears witness, it is astringent and at the same time bitter. It is, then, moderately astringent, but strongly bitter. It also loosens the belly, being one of the drugs called evacuant of excrement, so that from what has been said it is clear, if we remember at all what was demonstrated in the fourth book, that among drying drugs it is of the third degree, and among heating drugs either of the first degree in its intense form or of the second in its relaxed form. The particular actions also bear witness to the mixed character of its power. For the drug is good for the stomach, if any other is, and agglutinating of sinuses. It heals those ulcers which are hard to cicatrize, and especially those about the seat and the genitals. It also benefits inflammations of these when dissolved in water, and agglutinates wounds in the same manner. It is likewise suited, for one who uses it in the same way, to inflammations in the mouth and nostrils and eyes. And in general it is of a nature both to repel and to disperse at the same time, together with cleansing to a slight degree, to the extent that it is harmless to clean ulcers.

6.1.23 [23. On aloe.] Aloe. This herb does not grow much at all in our country, and the kind that grows in Great Syria is more watery and weaker in its power. Nevertheless it is naturally so drying that it agglutinates wounds. In the hotter regions, among which are Coele Syria and Arabia, it is much better. Best of all is the one in India, whose juice is this drug brought here and called aloe, which is of very great use because it dries without biting. It is not of a simple nature. As the taste also testifies, it is at once astringent and bitter: it is moderately astringent, but strongly bitter. It also loosens the bowel, being one of the drugs called eccoprotic. So from what has been said it is clear, if we remember anything of what was shown in the fourth book, that among drying drugs it is of the third order, and among heating drugs either of the first order intensified or of the second relaxed. Its particular effects also bear witness to the mixed character of its power. For the drug is good for the stomach, if anything is, and agglutinating of sinuses. It heals ulcers that are hard to cicatrize, especially those at the seat and the genitals. Dissolved in water, it also benefits their inflammations, and it agglutinates wounds in the same way. It is likewise suitable, for one who uses it in the same manner, against inflammations in the mouth, nose and eyes. In general it is naturally both repelling and dispersing at once, and also cleansing to a slight degree, so far as is harmless to clean ulcers.

In this way indeed it has often set in motion both urine and menses, whenever they are held back by a thick and viscous humour. 6.1.35 [λε΄. Περὶ ἀμπέλου μελαίνης.] Ἄμπελος μέλαινα. καλεῖται δὲ ἰδίως αὕτη βρυωνία, παραπλήσιός ἐστι τὰ πάντα τῇ προειρημένῃ πλὴν ἀσθενεστέρα. 6.1.36 [λστ΄. Περὶ ἀμυγδάλων.] Ἀμύγδαλα. τὰ μὲν πικρὰ φανερῶς τῆς λεπτυνούσης παντελῶς ἐστι δυνάμεως καὶ τῇ ποιότητι τεκμαιρομένῳ καὶ τῇ πείρᾳ κρίνοντι. περὶ μὲν οὖν τῆς πικρᾶς ποιότητος ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων εἴρηται· τῶν δὲ τῆς πείρας ἀρκεῖ δύο ταῦτα προχειρισαμένων ἐξ αὐτῶν τούτων διδαχθῆναι περὶ τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν. ἔφηλίν τε οὖν ἀποκαθαίρει καὶ ταῖς ἐκ θώρακός τε καὶ πνεύμονος ἀναπτύσεσι τῶν γλίσχρων τε καὶ παχέων χυμῶν ἱκανῶς συντελεῖ. ταῦτα δὲ ἡμῖν ἐδείκνυτο κατὰ γένος μὲν τῆς λεπτυντικῆς, κατ’ εἶδος δὲ τῆς ῥυπτικῆς ἔχεσθαι δυνάμεως. καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ ὅτι τῆς ἐκφρακτικῆς κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς εἴη ἂν δυνάμεως, ἐπιδέδεικται καὶ τοῦτο πρόσθεν. ἀλλὰ ἡ πεῖρα μαρτυρεῖ. τὰς γοῦν ἐν ἥπατι παχέων τε καὶ γλίσχρων χυμῶν ἐν τοῖς πέρασι τῶν ἀγγείων σφηνώσεις ἱκανῶς ἐκκαθαίρει. καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ τῶν πλευρῶν ἀλγήματα τὰ διὰ τὴν τοιαύτην αἰτίαν γιγνόμενα καὶ κατὰ σπληνὸς καὶ κώλου καὶ νεφρῶν ἰᾶται. καὶ τὸ δένδρον αὐτὸ σύμπαν ὁμοίαν ἔχει τὴν δύναμιν, ὥστε καὶ τούτου τὰς ῥίζας ἑφθὰς ἐπιπάττοντες ἀποκαθαίρουσιν ἐφήλεις. ὅσα δὲ γλυκέα τῶν ἀμυγδάλων, μετέχει μὲν καὶ ταῦτα βραχείας πικρότητος. ἀλλ’ ἐπικρατούσης τῆς γλυκύτητος ἀποκρύπτεται, κατάδηλον δ’ ἐναργῶς γίνεται χρονιζόντων αὐτῶν. ἐπιδέδεικται δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ὡς ἡ γλυκεῖα ποιότης θερμὴ συμμέτρως ἐστίν.

6.1.35 [35. On black vine.] Black vine. This one is properly called bryonia; it is in all respects similar to the one previously mentioned, except that it is weaker. 6.1.36 [36. On almonds.] Almonds. The bitter ones are manifestly of an altogether thinning power, both for one who infers from their quality and for one who judges by experience. Concerning the bitter quality, then, it has been spoken of in the fourth of these commentaries; and as for the evidence of experience, it suffices, when one has put forward these two instances, to be taught from these very facts about their power. For they clear away ephelis, and they contribute considerably to the expectoration from the chest and lung of viscous and thick humours. These effects, we showed, belong in genus to the thinning power, in species to the cleansing power. And indeed, that it would also be of the unblocking power incidentally, this too has been demonstrated previously. But experience bears witness. At any rate it adequately clears out the impactions of thick and viscous humours in the liver, in the extremities of the vessels. And indeed it also cures pains of the sides that arise from such a cause, and those in the spleen, colon and kidneys. And the tree itself as a whole has a similar power, so that people clear away ephelides by sprinkling on its roots boiled. As for those almonds that are sweet, these too partake of a slight bitterness; but since the sweetness prevails, it is concealed, though it becomes plainly evident when they age. It has been demonstrated in what precedes that the sweet quality is moderately hot.

6.1.35 [35. On the black vine.] Black vine. This is the one properly called bryōnia; it is similar in all respects to the one mentioned before, except that it is weaker. 6.1.36 [36. On almonds.] Almonds. The bitter ones are manifestly of an entirely thinning power, both to one who infers from their quality and to one who judges by experience. Now, the bitter quality has been discussed in the fourth of these commentaries. Of the evidence from experience, it is enough to bring forward these two instances and to learn from these very things about their power. They clean away freckles, and they contribute considerably to the bringing up, from the thorax and lung, of viscid and thick humours. These effects were shown by us to belong, by genus, to the thinning power, and, by species, to the cleansing power. But experience bears witness too: at any rate they thoroughly clear out the impactions of thick and viscid humours at the extremities of the vessels in the liver. As for the sweet almonds, these too share in a slight bitterness, but because the sweetness prevails it is hidden, and it becomes plainly evident when they have been kept a long time. Περὶ ἀνδράχνης.] Ἀνδράχνη ψυχρά ἐστι καὶ ὑδατώδης τὴν κρᾶσιν, ὀλίγου δέ τινος αὐστηροῦ μετέχει. διὸ καὶ ἀποκρούεται ῥεύματα καὶ μάλιστα χολώδη καὶ θερμὰ μετὰ τοῦ μεταβάλλειν αὐτὰ καὶ ἀλλοιοῦν κατὰ τὴν ποιότητα ἱκανῶς ἐμψύχειν. καὶ εἴη ἂν ἐν μὲν τῇ τοῦ ψύχειν δυνάμει τρίτης ἀποστάσεως ἀπὸ τῶν συμμέτρων τε καὶ μέσων, ἐν δὲ τῇ τοῦ ὑγραίνειν δευτέρας. ταῦτά τοι καὶ τοὺς καυσουμένους ὀνίνησιν εἴπερ τι ἄλλο κατά τε στόματος τῆς κοιλίας ἐπιτιθεμένη καὶ ὅλων τῶν ὑποχονδρίων, καὶ μάλιστα ἐπὶ τῶν ἑκτικῶν πυρετῶν, αἱμωδίας τέ ἐστιν ἴαμα ἐξηρασμένα ταχέως ὑπὸ τῆς τῶν ὀξέων χυμῶν ὁμιλίας αὐτὴ λειαίνουσά τε καὶ ἀναπληροῦσα, τῷ γλίσχρον ἔχειν τὴν ὑγρότητα. καὶ ὁ χυμὸς δὲ αὐτῆς ὁμοίως, ὥστε οὐ μόνον ἔξωθεν ἐπιτιθέμενος, ἀλλὰ καὶ πινόμενος ἐμψύχει. τοῦτο μέν γε καὶ αὐτῇ τῇ βοτάνῃ συμβέβηκεν ὅλῃ βρωθείσῃ. διὰ δὲ τὸ ὑποστύφειν καὶ δυσεντερικοῖς ἐστιν ἐπιτήδειον ἔδεσμα καὶ γυναικείῳ ῥῷ καὶ αἵματος ἀναγωγαῖς. εἰς ταῦτα μέντοι πολὺ δραστικώτερος αὐτῆς τῆς πόας ὁ χυλός ἐστιν.

6.1.43 [43. On andrachne.] Andrachne is cold and watery in its mixture, but it partakes of some small harsh element. Hence it also repels fluxes, and especially bilious and hot ones, together with changing them and altering them in quality by cooling sufficiently. And it would be, in its power of cooling, of the third degree of removal from the well-balanced and middle ones, and in that of moistening, of the second. For these reasons, indeed, it benefits those burning with fever as much as anything else, when applied over the mouth of the stomach and the whole of the hypochondria, and especially in the case of hectic fevers; and it is a remedy for haimodia, itself smoothing and filling up [the teeth] that have been quickly dried out by contact with acid juices, through having its moisture viscous. And its juice likewise, so that it cools not only when applied externally but also when drunk. This indeed also holds of the herb itself when eaten whole. And because of its being mildly astringent it is also a suitable food for dysenterics and for the female flux and for bringings-up of blood. For these purposes, however, the juice is much more effective than the herb itself.
Rendering B (opus-5-5) · unsure: μετὰ τοῦ μεταβάλλειν αὐτὰ καὶ ἀλλοιοῦν κατὰ τὴν ποιότητα ἱκανῶς ἐμψύχειν, ἐξηρασμένα, ὀξέων χυμῶν, καυσουμένους
6.1.43 [43. On purslane.] Purslane is cold and watery in its mixture, but it partakes of a small amount of something harsh. For this reason it both repels fluxes, especially bilious and hot ones, and, besides changing them and altering them in their quality, it cools sufficiently. It would be, in the power of cooling, of the third remove from the well-proportioned and median, and in that of moistening, of the second. For these reasons it benefits those suffering from ardent fever as much as anything else, when applied over the mouth of the stomach and the whole of the hypochondria, and especially in hectic fevers. It is also a remedy for teeth set on edge (haimōdia), itself swiftly smoothing and filling up [the parts] dried out by contact with the acid juices, because it has a viscous moisture. Its juice likewise, so that it cools not only when applied externally but also when drunk. This indeed also belongs to the plant itself when eaten whole. Because it is slightly astringent it is also a suitable food for dysenterics, and for the female flux and for bringings-up of blood. For these purposes, however, the juice is much more efficacious than the herb itself.

6.1.45 [με΄. Περὶ ἀνήθου.] Ἄνηθον θερμαίνει μὲν εἰς τοσοῦτον ὡς ἤτοι τῆς δευτέρας αὐτὸ τάξεως ἐπιτεταμένης ἢ τῆς τρίτης ἐκλελυμένης ὑπολαβεῖν. τῶν ξηραινόντων δὲ τῆς δευτέρας ἐστὶ τάξεως ἀρχομένης, ἢ τῆς πρώτης ἐπιτεταμένης, ὥστε εἰκότως ἐναφεψόμενον ἐλαίῳ, διαφορητικόν τε καὶ ἀνώδυνον καὶ ὑπνοποιὸν καὶ πεπτικὸν ὠμῶν καὶ ἀπέπτων ὄγκων ὑπάρχει. γίγνεται γὰρ τὸ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἔλαιον ἐγγύς τι τῆς κράσεως τοῖς πυοποιοῖς τε καὶ πεπτικοῖς ὀνομαζομένοις φαρμάκοις, πλὴν ὅτι θερμότερον αὐτῶν βραχεῖ καὶ λεπτομερές ἐστι καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ διαφορητικόν. καυθὲν δὲ τῆς τρίτης τάξεως γίνεται τῶν θερμαινόντων τε καὶ ξηραινόντων, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πλαδαροῖς ἕλκεσιν ἐπιπλαττόμενον ὀνίνησι καὶ μάλιστα τοῖς ἐν αἰδοίῳ. τὰ δὲ ἐπὶ τῆς πόσθης χρόνια καὶ ἐπουλοῖ καλῶς. ὑγρότερον δὲ δηλονότι καὶ ἧττον θερμόν ἐστι τὸ χλωρὸν ἔτι καὶ εὔχυμον, ὥστε πεπτικώτερον μὲν καὶ ὑπνοποιὸν ἔσται μᾶλλον τοῦ ξηροῦ, διαφορητικὸν δ’ ἧττον. διὰ τοῦτό μοι δοκοῦσι καὶ οἱ παλαιοὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ στεφάνοις χρῆσθαι παρὰ τὰ συμπόσια.

6.1.45 [45. On dill.] Dill heats to such a degree that one would suppose it to be either of the second order at its intensified degree or of the third at its relaxed degree. Among drying agents it is of the second order at its beginning, or of the first at its intensified degree, so that, reasonably enough, when boiled down in oil it is dispersing, pain-relieving, sleep-inducing, and concoctive of raw and unconcocted swellings. For the oil made from it comes somewhere near in mixture to the drugs called pus-producing and concoctive, except that it is a little hotter than they and fine-particled, and for this reason also dispersing. When burnt it becomes of the third order of heating and drying agents, and on this account, plastered upon flabby ulcers, it benefits them, and especially those on the genital member. The chronic ones on the prepuce it also cicatrizes well. The dill that is still green and full of juice is evidently moister and less hot, so that it will be more concoctive and more sleep-inducing than the dry, but less dispersing. For this reason the ancients too seem to me to have used garlands made from it at their drinking-parties.

6.1.45 [45. On dill.] Dill heats to such a degree that one may take it to be either of the second order at its intensified end or of the third at its relaxed end. Among drying agents it is of the second order at its beginning, or of the first at its intensified end, so that, as one would expect, when boiled in oil it is dispersing, anodyne, sleep-inducing, and concoctive of raw and unconcocted swellings. For the oil made from it comes close in mixture to the drugs called pus-producing and concoctive, except that it is slightly hotter than these and fine-particled, and for this reason also dispersing. When burnt, it becomes of the third order of heating and drying agents, and for this reason, applied as a plaster, it benefits flabby ulcers, and especially those on the genitals. And the chronic ones on the prepuce it also cicatrises well. The dill that is still green and full of juice is, clearly, moister and less hot, so that it will be more concoctive and more sleep-inducing than the dry, but less dispersing. For this reason, it seems to me, the ancients too used garlands made of it at symposia.

Περὶ ἀριστολοχίας.] Ἀριστολοχίας ἡ ῥίζα χρειωδεστάτη πρὸς τὰς ἰάσεις, πικρὰ καὶ ὑπόδριμυς ὑπάρχουσα. λεπτομερεστέρα δ’ ἐξ αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἡ στρογγύλη καὶ κατὰ πάντα δραστικωτέρα. τῶν δ’ ἄλλων δυοῖν ἡ μὲν κληματῖτις εὐωδεστέρα μὲν, ὥστε καὶ πρὸς τὰ μύρα χρῆσθαι τοὺς μυρεψοὺς αὐτῇ, πρὸς τὰς ἰάσεις δ’ ἀσθενεστέρα. ἡ μακρὰ δ’ ἧττον μὲν λεπτομερής ἐστι τῆς στρογγύλης, οὐ μὴν οὐδ’ αὐτή γε ἄπρακτος, ἀλλ’ ἔστι τῆς ῥυπτικῆς τε καὶ θερμαντικῆς δυνάμεως, καὶ τῆς στρογγύλης ἧττον μὲν ῥύπτει καὶ διαφορεῖ, θερμαίνει δ’ οὐχ ἧττον, ἀλλ’ ἴσως καὶ μᾶλλον. ὅθεν ἐφ’ ὧν μέν ἐστι χρεία τοῦ μετρίως ῥύπτειν, ἡ μακρὰ χρησιμωτέρα, καθάπερ ἔν τε ταῖς τῶν ἑλκῶν σαρκώσεσι καὶ ταῖς τῶν ὑστερῶν πυρίαις· ἐφ’ ὧν δὲ παχὺν χυμὸν ἰσχυρότερον λεπτῦναι, τῆς στρογγύλης ἡ χρεία. διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ δι’ ἔμφραξιν ἤ τι πάχος ἀπέπτων πνευμάτων ἀλγήματα θεραπεύει μᾶλλον ἡ στρογγύλη καὶ σκόλοπας ἀνάγει καὶ σηπεδόνας ἰᾶται καὶ τὰ ῥυπαρὰ τῶν ἑλκῶν καθαίρει καὶ ὀδόντας καὶ οὐλὰς λαμπρύνει. βοηθεῖ δὲ καὶ ἀσθματικοῖς καὶ λύζουσιν, ἐπιληπτικοῖς τε καὶ ποδαγρικοῖς, μεθ’ ὕδατος πινομένη, καὶ ῥήγμασι δὲ καὶ σπάσμασιν εἴπερ τι ἄλλο φάρμακον ἐπιτήδειός ἐστιν.
Rendering A (fable-5-1)
6.1.56 [56. On aristolochia (birthwort).] Aristolochia: its root is most useful for cures, being bitter and slightly pungent. Of these the round kind is more fine-particled and in every respect more active. Of the other two, the clematitis kind is more fragrant, so that the perfumers also use it for perfumes, but it is weaker for cures. The long kind is less fine-particled than the round, yet it too is not inactive, but is of a cleansing and heating power; and compared with the round it cleanses and disperses less, but heats no less, and perhaps even more. Hence in those cases where there is need of moderate cleansing the long kind is more useful, as in the fleshing-up of ulcers and in fomentations of the womb; but where a thick humour must be thinned more strongly, the round is what is needed. For this reason the round also treats better the pains that arise through obstruction or some thickness of unconcocted pneumata, and it draws out splinters and cures putrefactions and cleanses the foul kind of ulcers and brightens the teeth and gums. It also helps asthmatics and those suffering from hiccup, as well as epileptics and the gouty, when drunk with water; and for ruptures and spasms it is suitable, if indeed any other drug is.
Rendering B (opus-5-5) · unsure: οὐλὰς (as printed this is accusative plural of οὐλή, 'scar', the rendering used earlier in this work; with ὀδόντας and λαμπρύνει the sense requires 'gums', οὖλα, as in the parallel tradition, so the text is probably corrupt here), ἀπέπτων πνευμάτων (rendered 'unconcocted pneumata', i.e. undigested winds or flatus), σπάσμασιν (here taken as 'strains' of muscles, paired with ῥήγμασι, rather than 'spasms' or 'convulsions'), σαρκώσεσι (rendered 'filling-up with flesh', i.e. incarnation of ulcers)
6.1.56 [56. On aristolochia.] The root of aristolochia is most useful for cures, being bitter and somewhat pungent. Of its kinds, the round one is more fine-particled and in every respect more active. Of the other two, the clematitis is more fragrant, so that the perfumers even use it for their perfumes, but it is weaker for cures. The long one is less fine-particled than the round, yet it is not itself inactive either: it is of a cleansing and heating power. It cleanses and disperses less than the round, but it heats no less, and perhaps even more. Hence in cases where there is need of moderate cleansing the long one is more useful, as in the filling-up of ulcers with flesh and in fomentations of the womb. But in cases where a thick humour must be thinned more strongly, there is need of the round one. For this reason the round one also treats better the pains that arise from obstruction or from some thickness of unconcocted pneumata. It draws out splinters, heals putrefactions, cleans foul ulcers, and brightens the teeth and gums. Drunk with water, it also helps the asthmatic and those with hiccups, epileptics and gouty patients; and it is suited to ruptures and strains if any other drug is.

6.1.60 [ξ΄. Περὶ ἀρνογλώσσου.] Ἀρνόγλωσσον. μικτῆς καὶ τοῦτο κράσεώς ἐστιν. ἔχει μὲν γάρ τι καὶ ὑδατῶδες ψυχρὸν, ἔχει δέ τι καὶ αὐστηρὸν, ὅπερ ἐστὶ γεῶδες, ξηρὸν ψυχρὸν, ὥστε ψύχει τε ἅμα καὶ ξηραίνει καὶ κατ’ ἄμφω τῆς δευτέρας ἐστὶν ἀποστάσεως τῶν μέσων. ὅσα δὲ μετὰ ψύξεως ξηρά ἐστι φάρμακα, καὶ πρὸς ἕλκη κακοήθη πάντα καὶ πρὸς ῥεύματα καὶ σηπεδόνας ἁρμόττει. καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ πρὸς δυσεντερίας, καὶ γὰρ καὶ τὰς αἱμοῤῥαγίας ἵστησι καὶ, εἴ τι διακαὲς, ἐμψύχει, καὶ κολλητικὰ κόλπων ἐστὶ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἑλκῶν προσφάτων τε ἅμα καὶ παλαιῶν. ἐν ἅπασι δὲ σχεδὸν τοῖς τοιούτοις φαρμάκοις ἢ πρῶτον ἢ οὐδενὸς δεύτερον ἀρνόγλωσσον ὑπάρχει τῇ συμμετρίᾳ τῆς κράσεως. καὶ γὰρ ξηρότητος ἀδήκτου μετέχει καὶ ψύξεως μηδέπω ναρκούσης, καὶ ὁ καρπὸς δ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ αἱ ῥίζαι παραπλησίας εἰσὶ δυνάμεως, πλήν γε ὅτι ξηροτέρας τε καὶ ἧττον ψυχρᾶς. ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν καρπὸς λεπτομερέστερος, αἱ δὲ ῥίζαι παχυμερέστεραι. καὶ αὐτὰ δὲ τὰ φύλλα τῆς πόας ξηρανθέντα λεπτομερεστέρας τε καὶ ἧττον ψυχρᾶς γίγνεται δυνάμεως, ὡς ἀποπνεύσαντος αὐτῶν καὶ διαφορηθέντος τοῦ ὑδατώδους περιττώματος. ταῦτ’ ἄρα ταῖς μὲν ῥίζαις καὶ πρὸς ὀδόντων ἀλγήματα χρῶνται, διαμασωμέναις τε καὶ τοῖς διακλύμασιν αὐτῶν ἐνεψομέναις. πρὸς δὲ τὰς καθ’ ἧπαρ καὶ νεφροὺς ἐμφράξεις καὶ ταύταις μὲν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς φύλλοις καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἔτι τῷ καρπῷ. μετέχει γάρ τινος ἅπαντα ταῦτα δυνάμεως ῥυπτικῆς, ἣν εἰκὸς εἶναι κᾀν τῇ πόᾳ μὲν χλωρᾷ, νικᾶσθαι δ’ ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῆς ὑγρότητος.
Rendering A (fable-5-1)
6.1.60 [60. On arnoglosson.] Arnoglosson (plantain). This too is of a mixed mixture. For it has something watery and cold, and it also has something harsh, which is earthy, dry and cold, so that it cools and at the same time dries, and in both respects it is of the second degree of distance from the mean. Now all drugs that are dry together with coldness are suitable also for malignant ulcers, for fluxes and for putrefactions. And for this reason also for dysenteries; for indeed it also stops haemorrhages and, if anything is burning hot, it cools it, and it is agglutinating of sinuses and of other wounds, both fresh and old alike. And among almost all drugs of this kind arnoglosson is either first or second to none in the balanced proportion of its mixture. For it partakes of a dryness that does not bite and of a coldness that does not yet numb; and its seed and its roots are of a similar power, except that it is drier and less cold. But the seed is more fine-particled, while the roots are more coarse-particled. And the leaves themselves of the herb, when dried, become of a more fine-particled and less cold power, since their watery superfluity has evaporated and been dispersed. For this reason, then, they use the roots also for pains of the teeth, both chewed and boiled in mouth-rinses; and for obstructions in the liver and kidneys they use these too, but also the leaves, and still much more the seed. For all these partake of a certain cleansing power, which it is likely is present also in the green herb, but is overcome by the abundance of moisture.
Rendering B (opus-5-5) · unsure: διακλύμασιν (probably for διακλύσμασιν, 'mouthwashes'), ἐνεψομέναις, τῶν μέσων
6.1.60 [60. On plantain.] Plantain (arnoglosson). This too is of a mixed mixture. For it has something watery and cold, and it also has something harsh, which is earthy, dry and cold. So it cools and dries at the same time, and in both respects it is of the second remove from the median. All drugs that are dry together with cooling are suited to malignant ulcers, to fluxes and to putrefactions. On this account they are also suited to dysenteries, for they stop haemorrhages and, if anything is burning hot, they cool it; and they are agglutinating of sinuses and of the other ulcers, fresh and old alike. In nearly all such drugs plantain is either first or second to none in the due proportion of its mixture. For it partakes of a dryness that does not bite and of a coldness not yet numbing. Its fruit and its roots are also of a similar power, except that their power is drier and less cold. But the fruit is more fine-particled, and the roots more coarse-particled. The leaves of the herb themselves, when dried, also come to be of a more fine-particled and less cold power, since the watery residue has breathed out of them and been dispersed. For this reason people use the roots against toothaches as well, chewed and boiled in their mouthwashes. Against obstructions in the liver and kidneys they use these too, but also the leaves, and much more still the fruit. For all of these partake of a certain cleansing power, which is likely to be present in the green herb as well, but to be overcome by the quantity of its moisture.

6.1.72 [72. On atraktylis.] Atraktylis, or wild knēkos, is one of the thorny plants. This plant is of a drying and moderately hot power. 6.1.73 [73. On atraphaxis.] Atraphaxis is moist and cold in its mixture: moist in the second rank from the middle ones, and cold in the first, which indeed we said to be a tepid heat, such as the roses too possess, except that it has no share in astringency. 6.1.75 [75. On apsinthion.] Apsinthion possesses an astringent, a bitter and a pungent quality all at once, heating and at the same time cleansing, toning and drying. For this reason it both leads the bilious humours in the stomach away toward the downward evacuation and empties them out through the urine. And still more does it purge out through the urine what is bilious in the veins. For these reasons, when administered, it is of no benefit at all to phlegms contained in the stomach; and so likewise if they should happen to be in the chest and lung. For the astringent power in it is stronger than the bitter. But by virtue of partaking also of a certain pungency, it is hot in greater measure than it is cold. And if one had to define its mixture, taking it as a whole, according to the primary powers, even though it is non-uniform in its parts, we would say that it is hot of the first degree, but dry of the third. Its juice, however, is much hotter than the herb.

6.2.1 [α΄. Περὶ βαλάνου μυρεψικῆς.] Βάλανος μυρεψικὴ κομίζεται μὲν ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου, χρῶνται δ’ οἱ μυρεψοὶ τῷ τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῆς χυλῷ, θερμῷ τὴν δύναμιν ὄντι. τὸ δ’ ὑπόλοιπον ἀπόθλιμμα τὸ γεῶδες καὶ σκληρὸν ἐπικρατοῦσαν μὲν ἔχει τὴν πικρὰν ποιότητα. μέμικται δὲ τι καὶ στύψεως αὐτῷ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ῥυπτικήν τε ἅμα καὶ τμητικὴν καὶ συνακτικήν τε καὶ πιλητικὴν ἔχει τὴν ἐνέργειαν, ὥστε καὶ πρὸς ἰόνθους καὶ φακοὺς ἔφηλίν τε καὶ κνῆσιν, ἤδη δὲ καὶ πρὸς ψώραν καὶ λέπραν ἁρμόττει, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ σπλῆνας τήκει καὶ ἧπαρ σκιῤῥούμενον. εἰ δέ τις τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτῆς πίοι δραχμῆς ὁλκὴν μετὰ μελικράτου, ἐμετηρίου πειράσεται τοῦ φαρμάκου. πολλάκις δὲ καὶ διὰ τῆς κάτω κολίας ὑπάγει δαψιλῶς. ὅθεν ἐπειδὴ ὑπὲρ τοῦ διακαθῆραί τι τῶν σπλάγχνων καὶ μάλισθ’ ἧπαρ, ἢ σπλῆνα, τῷ φαρμάκῳ χρώμεθα, μετ’ ὀξυκράτου δίδομεν αὐτό. καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἄλλας δὲ τὰς ἐκτὸς ἐνεργείας ὄξει χαίρει μάλιστα. γίγνεται γὰρ δραστικὸν οὕτως, ὡς καὶ ψώρας καὶ λέπρας ἀποῤῥύπτειν, καὶ πολὺ δὴ μᾶλλον ἔτι τὰ τούτων ἐλάττω, φακοὺς, ἀλφοὺς, ἰόνθους, ἔφηλιν, ἀχώρας, ἐξανθήματα τὰ ἑλκώδη καὶ παχύχυμα πάντα. λαμπρύνει δὲ καὶ οὐλάς. ὅτι κᾀν τῷ καταπλάττειν αὐτῇ τὸν σπλῆνα κάλλιόν ἐστι μιγνύναι τι τῶν ξηραντικῶν ἀλεύρων, οἷόν ἐστιν ὀρόβινόν τε καὶ αἴρινον ἄλευρον, ἐκ τῆς περὶ συνθέσεως ἤδη φαρμάκων εἴη ἂν τοῦτο πραγματείας μᾶλλον, οὐ τῆς νῦν ἐνεστώσης, εἰρήσεται δὲ κᾀν τοῖς εὐπορίστοις. ἀρκεῖ δ’ ἐν τῷ παρόντι ῥυπτικήν τε καὶ τμητικὴν ἅμα στύψει τινὶ τὴν δύναμιν εἰπόντα τοῦ προειρη μένου φαρμάκου μεταβαίνειν ἐφ’ ἕτερον. ὁ μέντοι φλοιὸς αὐτοῦ πάνυ στυπτικός ἐστιν, ὥστε καὶ τούτῳ δύναιτ’ ἄν τις εἰς ὅσα περ ἰσχυρᾶς ἐστι χρεία στύψεως, εἰς ταῦτα χρῆσθαι.

6.2.1 [1. On the balanos myrepsike (ben-nut).] The balanos myrepsike (ben-nut) is brought from the barbarian land, and the perfumers use the juice of its flesh, which is hot in its power. The remaining pressed residue, the earthy and hard part, has the bitter quality predominating; but some astringency too is mixed in it, and for this reason it has an activity that is at once cleansing and cutting, and also contracting and compacting, so that it is suitable both for ionthoi and phakoi, ephelis and itching, and indeed also for psora and lepra; moreover, it also dissolves spleens and a liver that is becoming scirrhous. If someone were to drink a drachma's weight of its flesh with melikraton, he will experience the drug as an emetic; and often it also evacuates abundantly through the lower bowel. Hence, when we use the drug for the purpose of thoroughly cleansing one of the viscera, and especially the liver or the spleen, we give it with oxykraton. And for the other, external activities too it rejoices especially in vinegar; for in this way it becomes so effective as to cleanse away even psora and lepra, and much more still the conditions lesser than these—phakoi, alphoi, ionthoi, ephelis, achores, ulcerous eruptions and all those of thick humour. It also brightens scars. That, when plastering the spleen with it, it is better to mix in one of the drying meals, such as bitter-vetch and darnel meal, would belong rather to the treatise on the composition of drugs, not to the one now in hand; and it will be stated also in the Euporista. For the present it suffices, having said that the power of the aforementioned drug is cleansing and cutting together with a certain astringency, to pass on to another. Its bark, however, is very astringent, so that one could use this too for all those purposes for which there is need of strong astringency.

6.2.1 [1. On the perfumers' balanos.] The perfumers' balanos is brought from the barbarian country, and the perfumers use the juice of its flesh, which is hot in power. The remaining pressed residue (apothlimma), which is earthy and hard, has the bitter quality predominant. But something of astringency is also mixed in it, and for this reason it has an activity that is at once cleansing and cutting, and also contracting and condensing, so that it is suited to ionthoi, phakoi, ephelis and itching, and indeed also to psora and lepra; moreover it also melts spleens and a liver that is becoming scirrhous. If someone drinks a drachm's weight of the flesh itself with melikraton, he will experience the drug as an emetic. Often it also purges copiously through the lower belly. Hence, when we use the drug for the purpose of thoroughly cleansing one of the viscera, and especially the liver or the spleen, we give it with oxykraton. For its other, external activities too it does best with vinegar. For in this way it becomes so active as to cleanse away psora and lepra, and much more still the lesser of these conditions: phakoi, alphoi, ionthoi, ephelis, achores, and all eruptions that are ulcerous and of thick humours. It also brightens scars. That, when applying it as a cataplasm to the spleen, it is better to mix in some one of the drying meals, such as bitter-vetch meal and darnel meal, would belong rather to the treatise on the composition of drugs, not to the present one; but it will also be stated in the work on easily procured remedies. For the present it is enough to have said that the power of the aforementioned drug is cleansing and cutting together with a certain astringency, and to pass on to another. Its bark, however, is very astringent, so that one could use this too for all those purposes for which there is need of strong astringency.
