Περὶ βαλαυστίου.] Βαλαύστιον μὲν ἄνθος ἀγρίας ῥοιᾶς, οἷόν περ τῶν ἡμέρων ὁ κύτινος. ἰσχυρῶς δὲ στύφει τὴν γεῦσιν. καὶ δὴ καὶ ξηραντικῆς καὶ στυπτικῆς ἐστι δυνάμεως καὶ δηλονότι καὶ παχυμεροῦς, εἴ τι μεμνήμεθα τῶν ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων εἰρημένων, ἡνίκα ἐδείκνυμεν ἅπαν τὸ στῦφον γεῶδες εἶναι ψυχρόν. οὐδεμιᾶς δ’ ἔμφασιν ἔχει ποιότητος ἑτέρας, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἄν τις αὐτὸ θείη ξηραίνειν καὶ ψύχειν οὐκ ἀγεννῶς, εἴ γε δὴ μὴ κακῶς ἡμῖν ἐν τῷ τετάρτῳ τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων ἐδείκνυτο τοῖς γεώδεσι ψυχροῖς σώμασιν ὑπάρχειν ἡ στύφουσα ποιότης. ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ τὰ φαινόμενα μαρτυρεῖ. καὶ γὰρ εἰ παρατρίμμασι καὶ εἰ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἕλκεσιν ἐπιπάττοις αὐτὸ, τάχιστ’ ἂν ἴδοις εἰς οὐλὴν ἰόντα. ταῦτά τοι κᾀπὶ τῶν ἀναγόντων αἷμα δυσεντερικῶν, ἔτι τε τῶν κατὰ γαστέρα καὶ μήτραν ῥευμάτων, οὐκ ἔστιν ὅστις οὐ χρῆται τῷ φαρμάκῳ τούτῳ τῶν τὰς θεραπευτικὰς πραγματείας γραψάντων ἰατρῶν.

6.2.3 [3. On balaustion.] Balaustion is the flower of the wild pomegranate, just as kytinos is that of the cultivated ones. It is strongly astringent to the taste. And indeed it is of a drying and astringent power, and evidently also of a coarse-particled one, if we remember at all what was said in the fourth of these commentaries, when we showed that everything astringent is earthy and cold. It has no appearance of any other quality, and for this reason one would hold that it dries and cools in no mean degree, if indeed it was not wrongly demonstrated by us in the fourth of these commentaries that the astringent quality belongs to earthy cold bodies. And moreover the phenomena also bear witness. For if you sprinkle it upon chafings and upon other ulcers, you would very quickly see them proceeding to a scar. For these reasons, too, in the case of dysenteric patients who bring up blood, and further of fluxes in the belly and the womb, there is no one among the physicians who have written therapeutic treatises who does not use this drug.

6.2.4 [4. On bramble.] Of the bramble, the leaves, the shoots, the flower, the fruit and the root all partake of an astringent quality, and not obscurely. But they differ from one another in this: the leaves, and especially the soft and young ones, since they partake of a very large amount of water, are only slightly astringent. By the same reasoning the shoots too, so that when chewed they cure aphthae and the other ulcers in the mouth, and indeed are also able to glue together other wounds. For their mixture is composed of a cold earthy substance and a lukewarm watery one. The fruit, if it is ripe, partakes in no small measure also of the moderately hot juice, which is sweet, as we have shown, so that both for this reason and because of its moderate astringency it is edible and not unpleasant. The unripe fruit, however, is dominated by a cold earthy substance, and for this reason it is both acerbic and strongly drying. And indeed each of the two is also dried and stored away, being more drying than the fresh. The flower too is of the same power as the unripe fruit, (both being) drugs suitable for dysenteries and fluxes of the belly and atonies and spittings of blood. The root, in addition to being astringent, has further taken a share of no small amount of fine-particled substance, on account of which it also breaks up the stones in the kidneys.

6.2.15 [ιε΄. Περὶ βράθυος.] Βράθυ τῶν ἰσχυρῶς ξηραινόντων ἐστὶ, κατά γε τὰς τρεῖς ποιότητας ἃς καὶ τῷ γεύεσθαι διασημαίνει, παραπλησίως κυπαρίσσῳ, πλὴν ὅτι δριμύτερον αὐτῆς ἐστι καὶ ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις ἀρωματικώτερον. αὐτῆς τε οὖν ταύτης μετέχει τῆς ποιότητος ἧς εἴρηκα νῦν τῆς δριμείας, ἐπὶ θερμῇ κράσει συνισταμένης, ἔτι τε πικρότητός τε καὶ στύψεως ἀμυδροτέρας ἢ κατὰ κυπάρισσον. ὅσον γὰρ ἐν δριμύτητι πλεονεκτεῖ κυπαρίσσου, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ διαφορητικώτερον. κολλῆσαι μὲν οὖν οὐ δύναται διὰ ῥώμην ξηρότητος καὶ θερμότητος. εἰς τοσοῦτον γὰρ ἀμφοῖν τούτων μετείληφεν, ὡς ἤδη συντατικὸν καὶ φλογῶδες ὑπάρχειν· εἰς δὲ τὰς σηπεδόνας ὁμοίως ἁρμόττει κυπαρίσσῳ, καὶ μάλισθ’ ὅσαι κακοηθέστεραί τ’ εἰσὶ καὶ χρονιώτεραι. φέρουσι γὰρ ἀλύπως αὗται τὴν ἰσχὺν τοῦ φαρμάκου. καὶ τοίνυν καὶ τὰ μεμελασμένα καὶ τὰ λίαν ῥυπαρὰ μετὰ μέλιτος ἀποκαθαίρει καὶ ἄνθρακας ἀπολύει. διὰ δὲ τὴν λεπτομέρειαν καὶ καταμηνίων ἐστὶν ἀγωγὸν, εἴπερ τι καὶ ἄλλο, καὶ δι’ οὔρων αἷμα κινεῖ, καὶ τὰ ζῶντα τῶν ἐμβρύων διαφθείρει, τὰ νεκρὰ δ’ ἐκβάλλει. κείσθω δὴ καὶ τοῦτο τὸ φάρμακον ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν ἀποστάσεων κατά τε τὸ θερμαίνειν καὶ τὸ ξηραίνειν ἐν τοῖς μάλιστα λεπτομερέσιν ὑπάρχον. ταῦτ’ ἄρα καὶ μύροις μίγνυται καὶ μάλιστα τῷ γλευκίνῳ καὶ εἰς ἀντιδότους ἐμβάλλεται παμπόλλας. ἔνιοι καὶ ἀντὶ κινναμώμου διπλάσιον αὐτὸ βάλλουσι, λεπτυντικῆς τε γάρ ἐστι καὶ διαφορητικῆς εἰ ποθείη δυνάμεως.

6.2.15 [15. On brathy (savin).] Brathy is among the things that dry strongly, in respect at least of the three qualities which it also displays to the taste, in a manner similar to cypress, except that it is more pungent than it and, as one might say, more aromatic. It therefore partakes both of this very quality which I have just mentioned, the pungent, which is established upon a hot mixture, and further of a bitterness and an astringency fainter than in cypress. For in so far as it surpasses cypress in pungency, by so much also, for this reason, is it more dispersing. It is therefore not able to glue wounds together, because of the strength of its dryness and heat; for it has partaken of both of these to such a degree as to be already tensing and inflaming. But for putrefactions it is suitable in the same way as cypress, and especially for those that are more malignant and more chronic; for these bear without distress the strength of the drug. And accordingly it also cleanses, with honey, the parts that have turned black and those that are very foul, and detaches carbuncles. On account of its fineness of particles it is also a drawer-down of the menses, if anything is, and it moves blood through the urine, and it destroys living embryos and expels dead ones. Let this drug too, then, be placed in the third of the degrees of removal (ἀποστάσεων) in respect both of heating and of drying, being among the most fine-particled. For these reasons it is also mixed into unguents, and especially into the gleucine, and it is put into a very great number of antidotes. Some even put in double its amount in place of cinnamon, for it is of thinning and dispersing power if it is drunk.

6.2.15 [15. On brathy.] Brathy is one of the things that dry strongly, at least with respect to the three qualities which it also makes evident to the taste, much like cypress, except that it is more pungent than cypress and, as one might say, more aromatic. It therefore shares in this very quality I have just named, the pungent, which arises from a hot mixture, and further in bitterness and in an astringency fainter than that in cypress. For in so far as it exceeds cypress in pungency, it is for this reason also more dispersing. It cannot, then, glue [wounds] together, because of the strength of its dryness and heat. For it has partaken of both of these to such an extent as already to be tightening and fiery. For putrefactions, however, it is suited in the same way as cypress, and especially for those that are more malignant and more chronic, for these bear the strength of the drug without distress. And so, with honey, it also cleans out things that have become blackened and those that are very foul, and it detaches carbuncles. Because of its fineness of particles it is a promoter of the menses, if anything else is, and it moves blood through the urine, and it destroys living embryos and expels dead ones. Let this drug too, then, be placed in the third of the removes with respect to both heating and drying, being among the most fine-particled things. That is why it is both mixed into unguents, especially the gleucinum, and put into a great many antidotes. Some also put it in, in double quantity, in place of cinnamon, for it is of a thinning and dispersing power, should one want this.

Περὶ γλυκυρίζης.] Γλυκύριζα. τούτου τοῦ θάμνου τῶν ῥιζῶν ὁ χυλὸς μάλιστ’ ἐστὶ χρήσιμος ὁμοίως ταῖς ῥίζαις αὐτοῦ γλυκὺς ὑπάρχων, ἅμα βραχείᾳ τινὶ στύψει. διὸ καὶ τραχύτητας ἐκλεαίνειν πέφυκεν, οὐκ ἐν ἀρτηρίᾳ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν ψωρώδει κύστει, τῷ μετρίῳ τῆς κράσεως· εἴη ἂν οὖν ἡ φύσις αὐτοῦ οἰκεία τῆς ἡμετέρας κράσεως· τοιοῦτον γὰρ ἐδείχθη τὸ γλυκύ. προσούσης δέ τινος καὶ στύψεως ἡ σύμπασα κρᾶσις αὐτῆς, ὅσον ἐπὶ θερμότητι καὶ στύψει, κατὰ τὴν χλιαρὰν μάλιστα ἂν εἴη θερμασίαν, ἐγγυτάτω τῆς συμμέτρου. ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ ὑγρόν ἐστι τῇ κράσει τὸ μετρίως γλυκὺ, δεόντως ἄδιψόν ἐστι τὸ φάρμακον, ὑγρόν τε ἅμα μετρίως καὶ ψυχρότερον ὑπάρχον τῆς ἀνθρώπου φύσεως. φησὶ δ’ ὁ Διοσκουρίδης τὴν ῥίζαν ξηρὰν λεανθεῖσαν πτερυγίων ἐπιτήδειον γίνεσθαι κατάπαστον φάρμακον.

6.3.8 [8. On gloios.] Gloios is moderate and also softening. 6.3.9 [9. On glycyrrhiza.] Glycyrrhiza (liquorice). Of this shrub the juice of the roots is most useful, being sweet in the same way as its roots, together with a certain slight astringency. For this reason it is also naturally fitted to smooth roughnesses, not only in the windpipe but also in a scabby bladder, by the moderateness of its mixture; its nature, then, would be akin to our mixture, for the sweet was shown to be of this kind. But since a certain astringency is also present in it, its mixture as a whole, so far as concerns heat and astringency, would lie most of all in the region of lukewarm heat, very close to the well-proportioned. And since what is moderately sweet is also moist in its mixture, the drug is fittingly thirst-allaying, being at once moderately moist and colder than the nature of man. Dioscorides says that the root, when dry and finely ground, becomes a suitable drug to be sprinkled on for pterygia.

6.3.10 [10. On glycyside.] Glycyside, which they also call pentorobon and paeonia, has a root that is gently astringent with a certain sweetness, and, when chewed for longer, also with a slightly bitter pungency. Accordingly it both moves the menses, when drunk in the quantity of an almond with melikraton — one must, of course, pound it and sift it and so sprinkle it in; and it also clears out an obstructed liver and the kidneys. But these things it is naturally fitted to accomplish insofar as it is pungent and slightly bitter, whereas insofar as it also has something astringent, it stops the fluxes in the belly. In that case one must boil it down in one of the harsh wines and drink it. In general it is strongly drying in its power, so that I would not despair that it has with good reason been believed to cure the epilepsies of children even when hung about the neck. And indeed I once knew a child who for eight months was not seized at all from the time when he wore the root, but when the amulet somehow slipped off from his neck, he was at once seized, and when another was hung about him again, he was once more without complaint. It seemed to me better to remove it yet again for the sake of a test, and when we had done so, since he was convulsed again, we suspended a large and fresh piece of the root from his very neck, and from that point on, for the rest of the time, the boy became completely healthy and was no longer seized. It was reasonable, then, either that certain particles flowing off from the root, and then drawn in through inspiration, thus treat the affected places, or else that the air itself is turned and altered by the root. For in this way, too, the Cyrenaic juice benefits an inflamed uvula, and roasted melanthion manifestly dries catarrhs and coryzas, if someone, having tied it hot into a loose-woven linen cloth, continuously draws the heat from it through inspiration by the nostrils. And indeed, if you put several threads, and especially ones from marine purple, around a viper's neck and strangle the viper with them, and then hang each of the threads about the neck, it marvellously benefits the tonsils and whatever grows out around the neck. About such matters, then, I may perhaps go through separately at some time. But as for the mixture of peony, one must know that it is fine-particled and drying, yet not manifestly hot, but either well-balanced or hotter by some small degree.

6.3.10 [10. On glykysidē.] Glykysidē, which they also call pentorobos and paeonia, has a root that is gently astringent with some sweetness, and, when chewed for longer, also with a somewhat bitter pungency. For this reason it provokes the menses, when drunk in the amount of an almond with melicrat; one must, evidently, pound it and sift it and so sprinkle it on. It also cleanses out an obstructed liver and the kidneys. But these things it is naturally disposed to effect inasmuch as it is pungent and somewhat bitter; inasmuch as it also has something astringent, it stops the fluxes of the belly. In that case one must boil it down in one of the harsh wines and drink it. On the whole it is strongly drying in its power, so that I would not despair that it is with good reason believed to cure the epilepsies of children even when hung around them. And indeed I know of a little child who for eight months had no seizure at all from the time he wore some of the root; but when the amulet somehow fell off his neck, he was at once seized, and when another was hung around him again he was once more faultlessly well. It seemed better to me to remove it yet again for the sake of a trial, and having done so, when he was again convulsed, we hung a large and fresh piece of the root from his neck, and from then on for the rest of the time the boy became entirely healthy and was no longer seized. It was reasonable, then, either that certain particles flowing off from the root, and then drawn in through inhalation, heal in this way the affected places, or else that the air itself is turned and altered by the root. For so too the Cyrenaic juice benefits an inflamed uvula, and roasted melanthion manifestly dries catarrhs and coryzas, if one ties it while hot in a loose-woven linen cloth and continually draws in the heat from it through inhalation by the nostrils. And indeed, if you put several threads, especially ones dyed with sea purple, around the neck of a viper and strangle the viper with them, and then hang each of the threads around the neck, it wonderfully benefits paristhmia and whatever sprouts up about the neck. About such matters, then, I might perhaps go through them separately at some time. But one must know that the mixture of paeonia is fine-particled and drying, yet not manifestly hot, but either well-balanced or a little hotter.

6.4.9 [9. On dracontion.] Dracontion has something closely resembling aron both in its leaves and in its root. But it is more pungent than it and more bitter, and for this reason also both more heating and more fine-particled. It also has a certain slight astringency, and when this combines with the two qualities already mentioned, the pungent and the bitter, the drug becomes active in the highest degree. For indeed the root thoroughly cleanses all the viscera, thinning especially the thick and viscous humours, and it is the best drug for malignant ulcers; and it cleanses away and scours off, in general, both the other things that need cleansing and, with vinegar, alphoi. The leaves, having a similar power, are suitable for ulcers and for fresh wounds, and the less dry they are, the more they agglutinate; for the drier ones are more pungent in their power than is fitting for wounds. It is also believed to keep moist cheese free from putrefaction when placed around it on the outside, on account of the dryness of its mixture. The fruit is stronger not only than the leaves but also than the root, so that it is believed to melt away even cancers and polyps. And its juice cleanses away the things in the eyes.

Περὶ δρυός.] Δρυὸς ἅπαντα μὲν τὰ μόρια στυφούσης μετέχει ποιότητος, ἐπιπλέον δὲ τὸ ἐν τῷ φλοιῷ τοῦ πρέμνου τὸ ὑμενῶδες, καὶ τὸ ὑπὸ τῷ κελύφει τῆς βαλάνου, τὸ ἐπὶ τῇ σαρκὶ τοῦ καρποῦ. διὸ καὶ πρὸς ῥοῦν γυναικεῖον, αἵματός τε πτύσεις καὶ δυσεντερίας καὶ γαστρὸς ῥεύματα χρόνια χρήσιμον εἶναι πεπίστευται, μάλιστα δ’ ἀφέψοντες αὐτῷ χρῶνται. σφοδρότερον δ’ ἔτι στύφει φηγὸς καὶ πρῖνος, εἴτ’ οὖν εἴδη δρυὸς ὀνομάζειν αὐτά τις εἴτε καὶ διαφέρειν ὅλῳ τῷ γένει βούλοιτο. καὶ δὴ καὶ τὰ φύλλα τὰ μὲν τούτων τῶν φυτῶν ἁπαλὰ καταπλασσόμενα ξηραίνειν οὐκ ἀγεννῶς πέφυκε, τὰ δὲ τῆς ἑτέρας δρυὸς ἧττον, εἰς ὅσον καὶ στύψεως ἧττον μετείληφεν. ἔγωγ’ οὖν οἶδα καὶ κολλήσας ποτὲ τραῦμα δρεπάνῳ γεγονὸς, οὐδαμῶς ἑτέρου παρόντος φαρμάκου, τοῖς φύλλοις τῆς δρυός. ἔτριψα δ’ ἐπὶ πέτρας λείας αὐτὰ καὶ τὸ τραῦμα μετὰ τοῦ πέριξ χωρίου παντὸς κατέπλασα. ἔστι δὲ τῆς αὐτῆς τοῖς φύλλοις δυνάμεως καὶ ὁ καρπὸς τῆς δρυός. καὶ κέχρηνταί γε τούτῳ τινὲς τῶν ἰατρῶν ἐπὶ τῶν ἀρχομένων ἔτι καὶ αὐξανομένων φλεγμονῶν. ὅσαι γὰρ ἤδη σφοδραὶ τῶν στυφόντων οὐ δέονται. τὰ μὲν δὴ τοιαῦτα θεραπευτικῆς μᾶλλον ἢ τῆς ἐνεστώσης ἐστὶ πραγματείας. ἀπόχρη δ’ εἴς γε τὰ παρόντα γιγνώσκειν ὡς στυπτικῆς μὲν εἰς ὅσον εἴρηται μετείληφε δυνάμεως δρῦς, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ξηραντικῆς τε καὶ στυπτικῆς, θερμῆς δ’ ἐπ’ ὀλίγον εἶναι κατωτέρω τῶν μέσων ἐν τοῖς ὡς ἂν οὕτω τις εἴποι χλιαροῖς.

6.4.11 [11. On the oak.] All the parts of the oak share in an astringent quality, but to a greater degree the membranous part in the bark of the trunk, and that beneath the shell of the acorn, which lies upon the flesh of the fruit. Hence it has been believed to be useful for female flux, spittings of blood, dysenteries and chronic fluxes of the belly; and they use it chiefly by boiling it down. Still more vigorously astringent are the phegos and the prinos, whether one wishes to call them species of oak or to hold that they differ in their whole genus. And indeed the leaves of these plants, when tender and applied as a plaster, are by nature able to dry in no mean fashion, while those of the other oak less so, in proportion as it has partaken less of astringency. I myself, at any rate, know that I once glued together a wound made by a sickle, when no other drug at all was at hand, with the leaves of the oak. I ground them on a smooth stone and plastered the wound together with the whole surrounding region. The fruit of the oak too is of the same power as the leaves. And some of the physicians have used it for inflammations that are still beginning and increasing; for those that are already vigorous have no need of astringents. Such matters, however, belong to the therapeutic treatise rather than to the present one. For the present purposes it suffices to know that the oak has partaken of astringent power to the extent stated, and on this account of a drying and astringent power, but that in respect of heat it is a little below the middle things, among those which one might, so to speak, call tepid.

6.4.11 [11. On the oak.] All the parts of the oak share in an astringent quality, but to a greater degree the membranous part in the bark of the trunk, and that which lies under the shell of the acorn, upon the flesh of the fruit. For this reason it is also believed to be useful against female flux, spittings of blood, dysenteries and chronic fluxes of the belly; and people use it chiefly by boiling it down. The phēgos and the prinos are still more vehemently astringent, whether one wishes to call them species of oak or to hold that they differ in their whole genus. Moreover, the tender leaves of these plants, applied as a poultice, are by nature able to dry not ignobly, but those of the other oak less so, in proportion as they also partake less of astringency. I myself, at any rate, know that I once agglutinated a wound made by a sickle with the leaves of the oak, when no other drug at all was at hand. I ground them on a smooth stone and plastered them over the wound together with the whole surrounding region. The fruit of the oak is also of the same power as the leaves. And some physicians have in fact used it for inflammations that are still beginning and increasing; for those that are already intense do not require astringents. But such matters belong to the therapeutic treatise rather than to the present one. For present purposes it suffices to know that the oak partakes of an astringent power to the extent stated, and for this reason of a drying and astringent one, and that it is hot to a slight degree, below the middle ones, among those which, as one might put it, are lukewarm.

ἐκτείνηται τοῦ σώματος καὶ ἑαυτῷ μένῃ συνεχὲς, ἀναπίνηταί τε πρὸς τοῦ χρωτὸς, ἡγεῖσθαι τοῦτο κάλλιστόν τε καὶ τὴν ἐλαίου μάλιστα κεκτημένον ἀρετὴν, οἷόν πέρ ἐστι τὸ Σαβῖνον. ὅτι δὲ τὸ πεπλυμένον ἔλαιον ἀδηκτότατόν ἐστιν εἴρηται καὶ πρόσθεν. ὅπως δ’ ἄν τις κάλλιστα πλύνοι, διὰ τῆς ἐφεξῆς ἐρῶ πραγματείας τῆς περὶ συνθέσεως φαρμάκων· ἔνθα καὶ περὶ Σικυωνίου καὶ εἴ τι τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν ἔλαιον εἰρήσεται. νυνὶ δὲ περὶ τῶν ἁπλῶν διέξειμι καὶ προσθήσω ἤδη τὸν περὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐλαίων λόγον. ὀνομάζεται γὰρ δή τι καὶ κίκινον ἔλαιον, ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μάλιστα γιγνόμενον, ἐκ τοῦ καρποῦ τοῦ κίκεως, καὶ ῥαφάνινον δὴ καὶ σησάμινον, ἀμυγδάλινόν τε καὶ καρύϊνον, ἔτι τε σινάπινον, σχίνινον, δάφνινον, μελάνθινον, τερμίνθινον, μαστίχινον, μύρσινον, βαλάνινον, ὑοσκυάμινον, ἄλλα τε πρὸς τούτοις οὐκ ὀλίγα τῶν καρπῶν ἐκθλιβόμενα πάντα. διαφέρει δ’ ἀλλήλων ταῦτα τὰς αὐτὰς διαφορὰς ἅσπερ καὶ οἱ καρποί. τὸ μὲν γὰρ κίκινον λεπτομερέστερόν τε καὶ διαφορητικώτερόν ἐστιν, ὅμοιον μάλιστα τῷ ἐκ τῆς ἐλαίας ἐλαίῳ τῷ παλαιῷ. διὸ καὶ χρηστέον ἔνθ’ ἂν ᾖ κίκινον ἔλαιον γεγραμμένον ἔν τινι συνθέσει φαρμάκου, μὴ παρόντος αὐτοῦ, τῷ κοινῷ ἐλαίῳ, καὶ μάλιστ’ εἰ Σαβῖνον εἴη. τὸ δὲ ῥαφάνινον ὅμοιον μὲν τἄλλα τῷδε, θερμότερον δὲ, καὶ τούτου μᾶλλον ἔτι τὸ σινάπινον. ὅμοιον δὲ αὐτῷ τὸ ἐκ τοῦ μελανθίου. ἔμπαλιν δὲ τούτοις τὸ μύρσινόν τε καὶ σησάμινον, τὸ μὲν τῷ στύφειν, τὰ δ’ ὅτι παχυμερῆ. μικτῆς δέ ἐστι δυνάμεως τό τε σχίνινον καὶ τὸ τερμίνθινον καὶ τὸ μαστίχινον, οὐ γὰρ μαλάττει μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ στύφει. τὸ δ’ ἀμυγδάλινον ἐπικρατοῦσαν μὲν ἔχει τὴν πικρότητα, μετέχει δέ τινος καὶ στύψεως, οὐ μὴν τό γε καρύϊνον, ἀλλ’ ἁπλῆς μάλιστα δυνάμεώς ἐστι τοῦτο τῆς διαφορητικῆς. θερμότερον δ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ διαφορητικώτερον ὑπάρχει τὸ δάφνινον, καὶ τούτου μᾶλλον ἔτι τὸ κέδρινον. ἐγγὺς δ’ αὐτῷ τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ὑγρᾶς πίττης τὸ δάδινον, ἧττον μὲν τοῦ δαφνίνου θερμὸν, ξηραίνει δὲ μᾶλλον. τὸ δ’ ὑοσκυάμινον μικτῆς ἐστι δυνάμεως, μαλακτικῆς τε ἅμα καὶ ψυκτικῆς. τὸ δὲ κίκινον ἔλαιον ὑπάγει γαστέρα. τοῦτου δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον τὸ ἐκ τοῦ κνιδίου κόκκου, καὶ τοσούτῳ γε μᾶλλον ὅσῳ ὁ κόκκος αὐτοῦ τοῦ κίκους καθαρτικώτερος ὑπάρχει. ἔστι δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀγρίας ἐλαίας ἔλαιον οὐχ ἁπλῆς κράσεως, ἀλλὰ ῥυπτικόν τε ἅμα καὶ στυπτικόν. αὐχμηρότερον δ’ ὡς ἐν ἐλαίοις τοῦτο καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο τὸ Ἰστρικόν. ἐφεξῆς δ’ αὐτοῖς τὸ Σπανόν. λιπαρώτατον δὲ τό τε Λιβυκόν ἐστι καὶ τὸ Κιλίκιον, ἅμα δὲ λιπαρόν τε καὶ λεπτομερὲς τὸ Σαβῖνον. ἐν τῷ μέσῳ δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων ἁπάντων τό τε κατὰ τὰς Κυκλάδας νήσους ἐστὶ καὶ τὴν Ἑλλάδα καὶ τὴν Ἀσίαν. κρίνεται δὲ τὸ μὲν λιπαρὸν ἔλαιον τῇ γλισχρότητι, τὸ δὲ λεπτομερὲς τῷ τε διαυγεῖ καὶ καθαρῷ, καὶ τῷ πλεῖστον ἀλείφεσθαι τοῦ σώματος ὑπ’ ἐλαχίστου καὶ τῷ πρὸς τοῦ χρωτὸς ἀναπίνεσθαι ῥᾳδίως. ἐκ δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων ἔνεστί σοι καὶ περὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐλαίων, ὁπόσα τοῖς μύροις ὁμωνύμως λέγεται, γιγνώσκειν ἤδη, λέγω δὲ ῥοδίνου τε καὶ μηλίνου καὶ κρινίνου καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα καρπῶν ἢ ἀνθῶν ἢ βλαστῶν ἢ φύλλων ἐναποβρεχομένων ἐν ἐλαίῳ γίγνεται. τούτων γὰρ ἕκαστον, ὅταν ἅμα τοῖς ἀρώμασι σκευασθῇ, μύρον ἀποτελεῖται. λεχθήσεται δ’ ἐπιπλέον ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐν τῆ περὶ συνθέσεως φαρμάκων πραγματείᾳ. τὸ δ’ εἰς τὸν παρόντα χρήσιμον εἰπὼν ἀπαλλάξομαι. κατὰ φύσιν ἑκάστου τῶν ἐμβληθέντων ἀλλοιωθήσεται τὸ ἔλαιον. ἐξ ὧν οὖν ὑπὲρ ἑκάστου τῶν ἐμβαλλομένων ἐν τῷδε τῷ λόγῳ παντὶ καθόλου μανθάνεις, ἐκ τούτων ἂν εἴη σοι καὶ περὶ τοῦ καθέκαστον αὐτῶν ἐλαίου γιγνώσκειν.

6.5.4 [4. On olive oil.] Oil: that from the olive, which we also call oil in the most proper sense, has had the nature of its mixture determined in the preceding books; for it was shown to be moistening and moderately hot. Such is the sweetest oil, produced especially from tree-ripened fruit. But the oil called raw-pressed and omphacine (from unripe olives), to the degree that it partakes of astringency, to that same degree partakes also of coldness. As for old oil, that which comes from sweet oil grown old is hotter and more dispersing, whereas that from raw-pressed oil, so long as it preserves something of its astringency, is of mixed power, but when it has completely cast this off, it becomes like the other. And indeed those who in the preparation throw in olive-shoots also produce an oil resembling the omphacine. One ought not to inquire how it has been prepared, but rather taste it oneself: if it shows any astringency, one should suppose that to the degree it partakes of this, to that same degree it partakes also of coldness, as does the oil brought from Iberia, which they call Spanish; but if on tasting it shows no astringency at all, but is perfectly sweet, one should consider this to be moderately hot. And if it also appears fine-particled—such is the oil that is pure and translucent to the eye, and when a small quantity, once taken up, spreads over the greatest extent of the body and remains continuous with itself, and is drunk up by the skin—one should consider this the finest and the oil that most fully possesses the excellence of oil, of the kind that the Sabine oil is. That washed oil is the least biting has been stated earlier too; and how one may best wash it I shall say in the following treatise, that on the composition of drugs, where there will also be a discussion of the Sicyonian oil and of any other such oil. For now I am going through the simple drugs, and I shall now add the account of the other oils. For there is named also a castor oil (kikinon), produced especially in Egypt, from the fruit of the kiki, and radish-seed oil, and sesame oil, almond oil and walnut oil, and further mustard oil, mastic-tree (schinos) oil, laurel oil, melanthion (black cumin) oil, terebinth oil, mastic oil, myrtle oil, ben-nut (balanos) oil, henbane oil, and not a few others besides these, all pressed out from fruits or seeds. These differ from one another by the same differences as the fruits themselves. For castor oil is more fine-particled and more dispersing, most like old oil from the olive; hence, wherever castor oil is prescribed in some composition of a drug, if it is not available one should use the common oil, and especially if it be Sabine. Radish-seed oil is in other respects like this one, but hotter, and mustard oil hotter still than this; like the latter is the oil from melanthion. Contrary to these are myrtle oil and sesame oil, the former by being astringent, the latter because they are coarse-particled. Of mixed power are mastic-tree oil, terebinth oil and mastic oil, for they not only soften but are also astringent. Almond oil has bitterness predominating, but partakes also of some astringency; not so walnut oil, however, which is of a single, simple power, the dispersing. Hotter and more dispersing than it is laurel oil, and cedar oil more so still than this; near to the latter is the oil from liquid pitch, pine-resin oil (dadinon), less hot than laurel oil but more drying. Henbane oil is of mixed power, at once softening and cooling. Castor oil loosens the belly, and the oil from the Cnidian berry still more than this, and so much the more as its berry is more purgative than the kiki itself. The oil from the wild olive, too, is not of a simple mixture, but at once cleansing and astringent. This is the driest, as oils go, and after it the Istrian, and next to these the Spanish. The oiliest are the Libyan and the Cilician, while the Sabine is at once oily and fine-particled; in the middle of all those mentioned lies the oil of the Cycladic islands, Greece and Asia. Oily oil is judged by its viscosity, fine-particled oil by its translucency and purity, by the greatest extent of the body being anointed by the smallest quantity, and by its being readily drunk up by the skin. From what has been said you can now also know about the other oils, as many as are called by the same names as the perfumes—I mean rose oil, quince oil, lily oil, and all such as are made by steeping fruits or flowers or shoots or leaves in oil. For each of these, when prepared together with aromatics, is made into a perfume. More will be said about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs; having said what is useful for the present purpose, I shall take my leave. The oil will be altered according to the nature of each of the things thrown into it. From what you learn about each of the things thrown in, throughout this whole work in general, from these you would be able to know also about the oil of each of them individually.

6.5.4 [4. On oil.] Of oil, the kind that comes from the olive, which we also call oil in the most proper sense, what sort of thing it is in its mixture has been determined in the preceding discussions: it was shown to be moistening and moderately warm. Such is the sweetest oil, produced above all from fruit that has fallen ripe from the tree (drupetēs). The oil called 'raw-pressed' (ōmotribes) and omphacine partakes of cooling to the same extent that it has taken a share of astringency. As for old oil, that which arises from sweet oil growing old is warmer and more dispersing. That which arises from raw-pressed oil is of mixed power so long as it preserves some of its astringency, but when it loses this completely it becomes like the other. Moreover, those who add olive shoots during the preparation also produce an oil similar to omphacine oil. One should not enquire how it has been prepared, but taste it oneself. If it shows some astringency, one should suppose that it shares in cooling to the same extent that it partakes of astringency, as is the case with the oil brought from Iberia, which they call Spanish. But if on tasting it appears not to be astringent at all, and is exactly sweet, one should consider it moderately warm. And if it also appears fine-particled, one should consider it the finest and the one possessing above all the excellence of oil, such as the Sabine is. Fine-particled oil is that which looks pure and translucent, and which, when a small amount is taken, is spread over a very large part of the body, remains continuous with itself, and is drunk up by the skin. That washed oil is the least biting has also been said before. How one might best wash it I shall tell in the following treatise, the one on the composition of drugs; there I shall also speak about Sicyonian oil and any other such oil. For now I am going through the simple drugs, and I shall next add the account of the other oils. There is also an oil called kikinon, produced mostly in Egypt from the fruit of the kiki, and there are radish oil and sesame oil, almond oil and nut oil, and further mustard oil, lentisk oil, laurel oil, melanthium oil, terebinth oil, mastic oil, myrtle oil, balanos oil, henbane oil, and not a few others besides these, all pressed out of fruits. These differ from one another by the same differences as the fruits do. Kikinon oil is more fine-particled and more dispersing, very similar to the old oil from the olive. Therefore, wherever kikinon oil is written in some composition of a drug and it is not available, one should use common oil, especially if it is Sabine. Radish oil is similar to this in other respects but warmer, and mustard oil is still more so than this. Similar to it is the oil from melanthium. Opposite to these are myrtle oil and sesame oil, the former because it is astringent, the latter because it is coarse-particled. Lentisk oil, terebinth oil and mastic oil are of mixed power, for they do not only soften but are also astringent. Almond oil has bitterness predominating, but it also partakes of some astringency. Nut oil does not; it is above all of a simple power, the dispersing one. Laurel oil is warmer and more dispersing than it, and cedar oil is still more so than this. Close to it is the torch-wood oil (dadinon) from liquid pitch, which is less warm than laurel oil but dries more. Henbane oil is of mixed power, at once softening and cooling. Kikinon oil loosens the belly. The oil from the Cnidian berry does so still more than this, and more by as much as the berry is more purgative than the kiki itself. The oil from the wild olive is also not of a simple mixture, but at once cleansing and astringent. For an oil, this one is rather dry (auchmēroteron), and after it comes the Istrian. Next to these comes the Spanish. The most oily are the Libyan and the Cilician, while the Sabine is at once oily and fine-particled. In the middle of all those mentioned is the oil of the Cyclades islands, of Greece and of Asia. Oily oil is judged by its viscidity. Fine-particled oil is judged by its translucency and purity, by a very large part of the body being anointed by a very small amount, and by its being readily drunk up by the skin. From what has been said you are now able to know also about the other oils that are called by the same names as the perfumes, I mean rose oil, quince oil, lily oil, and all such as are made by steeping fruits, flowers, shoots or leaves in oil. For each of these, when prepared together with aromatics, is made into a perfume. More will be said about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs. Having said what is useful for the present purpose, I shall finish. The oil will be altered according to the nature of each of the things put into it. You learn in general about each of these ingredients throughout this whole account, and from this you will be able to know also about the oil of each of them individually.

6.5.7 [7. On helenium.] Of the herb helenium it is the root that is most useful. It does not heat immediately at the first application, and for this reason it must be said to be not strictly hot and dry, as black and white pepper are, but hot and dry together with a residual moisture. For this reason too it is suitably mixed into the linctuses used for the bringing up of the viscid and thick humours in the chest and lung, and with it they redden the parts troubled by cold and chronic affections, such as certain cases of ischias, hemicranias, and continual dislocations of certain joints owing to moisture.

6.5.10 [10. On helxine.] Helxine, which some call perdikion, others parthenion, others sideritis, and there are those who call it Herakleia. Its power is cleansing and gently astringent, together with a somewhat cold moisture. Hence it heals all inflammations both at their beginning and in their increase up to the peak, and especially the hot ones. And indeed it is also applied as a plaster to incipient phygethla. Its juice, too, with rose-oil, is moderately suited to inflammatory pains of the ears. Some also gargle with it for affections of the tonsils, and certain physicians have given it to those with chronic coughs. Of its cleansing power it gives clear evidence also in the case of glass vessels.

Hence it heals all inflammations at their beginning and during their increase up to the peak, and especially the hot ones. 6.5.21 [21. On erysimon.] The seed of erysimon, just as in taste it appears closely similar to kardamon (cress), so too in its power is fiery and heating. It is useful, together with lincti, for the expectoration of viscous and thick humours in the region of the thorax and lung. Περὶ ζιγγιβέρεως.] Ζιγγιβέρεως ἡ ῥίζα χρήσιμός ἐστιν, ἥνπερ δὴ κομίζουσιν ὡς ἡμᾶς ἐκ τῆς βαρβάρου. θερμαίνει μὲν οὖν ἰσχυρῶς, ἀλλὰ οὐ κατὰ τὴν πρώτην προσβολὴν ὡς τὸ πέπερι. ταύτῃ τοι καὶ λεπτομερέστερον ἧττον αὐτὸ πεπέρεως ὑποληπτέον ὑπάρχειν. ἐλύετο γὰρ ἂν εἰς λεπτὰ μόρια καὶ διὰ ταχέων ἐνεργείᾳ θερμὸν ἐγίγνετο, καθάπερ ἐκεῖνο. φαίνεται γοῦν ἀκατεργάστου τινὸς ἔτι καὶ παχυμερεστέρας οὐσίας μετέχον καὶ ταύτης οὐ ξηρᾶς καὶ γεώδους, ἀλλ’ ὑγρᾶς καὶ ὑδατώδους μᾶλλον. διὰ τοῦτό γέ τοι καὶ τιτρᾶται ῥᾳδίως, ὅτι μέτεστιν αὐτῆς περιττωματικῆς ὑγρότητος. οὐδὲν γοῦν τοῦτο πάσχει τῶν ἤτοι ξηρῶν ἀκριβῶς ἢ ὑγρῶν μὲν, ἀλλὰ τῶν κατειργασμένην τε καὶ οἰκείαν ἐχόντων ὑγρότητα. ταὐτὸν τούτῳ καὶ τὸ μακροπέπερι πεπονθὸς, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο παραμένει μέχρι πλείονος ἡ ἀπὸ ζιγγιβέρεως καὶ μακροπεπέρεως θερμότης ἤπερ ἡ ἀπὸ λευκοῦ τε καὶ μέλανος. ὡς γὰρ ἡ ἀπὸ τῶν ξηρῶν καλάμων φλὸξ ἀνάπτεται μὲν ἅμα, καὶ πάντῃ σκίδναται τάχιστα, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον καὶ ἡ ἀπὸ τῶν ξηρῶν τῇ δυνάμει φαρμάκων. ἡ δ’ ἀπὸ τῶν ὑγροτέρων ἀνάλογον τοῖς χλωροῖς ξύλοις καὶ βραδύτερον ἐξάπτεται καὶ παραμένει μέχρι πλείονος, ὅθεν καὶ ἡ χρεία διάφορος ἑκατέρου τῶν φαρμάκων. ὅταν μὲν γὰρ τὸ πᾶν σῶμα῾ ἐκθερμῆναι βουλώμεθα διὰ ταχέων, ὅσα ταχέως μὲν ἐκθερμαίνει πλησιάζοντα τῷ τοῦ ζώου θερμῷ, ταχέως δὲ πάντῃ φέρεται δοτέον. ἐπειδὰν δέ τι μόριον ἐψυγμένον ἐκθερμῆναι βουληθῶμεν, ἔμπαλιν πρακτέον, ὅσα βραδέως θερμαινόμενα μέχρι πλείστου παραμένει, ταῦτα προσφέρονται. τὸ μὲν οὖν ζιγγίβερι καὶ τὸ μακροπέπερι, κᾂν εἰ διαφέρει ταύτῃ τοῦ μέλανος πεπέρεως, ἀλλ’ ἐπ’ ὀλίγον. κάρδαμον δὲ καὶ νᾶπυ καὶ θαψία καὶ ὁ τῶν ἀγρίων περιστερῶν ἀπόπατος ἐν χρόνῳ τε πλείονι τελέως ἐκπυροῦται καὶ μέχρι πλείστου παραμένει.

6.6.1 [1. On zeia.] Zeia is somehow intermediate in its whole power between wheat and barley, so let it be known from those. 6.6.2 [2. On ginger.] Of ginger the root is what is useful, which indeed they bring to us from the barbarian land. It heats, then, strongly, but not at the first contact, as pepper does. For this very reason one must also suppose it to be less fine-particled than pepper. For otherwise it would be dissolved into fine parts and would quickly become hot in actuality, as that one does. At any rate it appears to partake of some substance that is still unworked and coarser-particled, and this not dry and earthy but rather moist and watery. For this reason, indeed, it is also easily bored through, because it has a share of superfluous moisture. At any rate none of the things that are either precisely dry, or moist but possessing a moisture that is worked up and proper to them, suffers this. Long pepper too has undergone the same thing as this, and for this reason the heat from ginger and long pepper persists for longer than that from white and black pepper. For just as the flame from dry reeds is kindled all at once and is scattered in every direction most quickly, in the same way too is the flame from drugs that are dry in their power. But that from the moister ones, by analogy with green wood, is both kindled more slowly and persists for longer; whence also the use of each of the two kinds of drugs is different. For when we wish to heat the whole body quickly, one must give those which heat quickly on coming near the heat of the animal and are quickly carried in every direction. But when we wish to heat some chilled part, one must act the opposite way: those which, heating slowly, persist for the longest, these are applied. Now ginger and long pepper, even if they differ in this respect from black pepper, yet differ only slightly. But kardamon and mustard and thapsia and the dung of wild pigeons both become fully ignited over a longer time and persist for the longest.

6.6.1 [1. On zeia.] Zeia is, in its whole power, somewhere between wheat and barley, so let it be known from those. 6.6.2 [2. On ginger.] The root of ginger is the useful part; it is this that they bring to us from the barbarian country. It heats strongly, but not at the first contact, as pepper does. For this very reason one must suppose that it is less fine-particled than pepper. For otherwise it would be dissolved into fine particles and would quickly become hot in actuality, as that does. It appears, at any rate, to contain a substance that is still somewhat unconcocted and more coarse-particled, and this not dry and earthy, but rather moist and watery. It is for this reason too that it is readily worm-eaten, because it contains residual moisture. None of those things that are either exactly dry, or moist but possessing a concocted and proper moisture, suffers this. Long pepper is affected in the same way, and for this reason the heat from ginger and long pepper persists longer than that from white and black pepper. For just as the flame from dry reeds catches all at once and very quickly spreads in every direction, so too does the heat from drugs that are dry in power. That from the moister ones, analogously to green wood, both kindles more slowly and persists longer; hence the use of each kind of drug is also different. For when we wish to heat the whole body quickly, we must give those things which heat quickly on coming into contact with the animal's heat, and which are quickly carried in every direction. But when we wish to heat some chilled part, we must do the opposite: those things which, being heated slowly, persist for a very long time are the ones applied. Ginger and long pepper, then, even if they differ from black pepper in this respect, do so only slightly. But cress, mustard, thapsia and the dung of wild pigeons both become fully fiery over a longer time and persist for a very long time.

Περὶ ἡδυόσμου.] Ἡδύοσμον, ἔνιοι δὲ μίνθην προσαγορεύουσιν. ἔστι γὰρ ἑτέρα τις οὐκ εὐώδης μίνθη, ἣν καὶ καλαμίνθην καλοῦσι. δριμεῖαι δ’ εἰσὶ γευομένοις ἀμφότεραι καὶ θερμαὶ τὴν δύναμιν ἐκ τῆς τρίτης που τάξεως τῶν θερμαινόντων. ἀσθενεστέρα μὴν ἡ εὐώδης μίνθη τῆς καλαμίνθης ἐστὶ καὶ ἧττον θερμαντική. καθόλου γὰρ εἰπεῖν ἡ μὲν ὥσπερ ἀγρία τίς ἐστιν, ἡ δ’ ἥμερος, ὥστε διὰ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ κηπεύεσθαι προσοῦσαν ὑγρότητα καὶ πρὸς ἀφροδίσια παρορμᾷ μετρίως. ὑπάρχει δὲ τοῦτο κοινὸν ἅπασιν οἷς μέτεστιν ὑγρότητος ἡμιπέπτου τε καὶ φυσώδους. διὰ δὲ τὴν τοιαύτην τῆς πόας κρᾶσιν καὶ κατὰ τῶν ἀποστημάτων ἐπιτιθέασιν ἔνιοι μετ’ ἀλφίτων αὐτὴν, ὅπερ ἡ καλαμίνθη ποιεῖν οὐ δύναται τῷ σφοδρότερον ἢ τὰ τοιαῦτα θερμαίνειν καὶ ξηραίνειν. ἔχει δέ τι καὶ πικρὸν καὶ στρυφνὸν ἐν ἑαυτῇ, καὶ τῷ μὲν πικρῷ τὰς ἕλμινθας ἀναιρεῖ, τῷ δὲ στρυφνῷ μετ’ ὀξυκράτου πινομένη τὰς προσφάτους αἵματος ἀναγωγὰς ἐπέχει. λεπτομερὴς δ’ ἐστὶ τὴν οὐσίαν εἴπερ τις καὶ ἄλλη πόα.

6.7.1 [1. On hedyosmon (mint).] Hedyosmon (mint), which some call minthe. For there is another, non-fragrant minthe, which they also call kalaminthe (calamint). Both are pungent to those who taste them and hot in their power, from roughly the third rank of heating things. Yet the fragrant minthe is weaker than kalaminthe and less heating. For, to speak generally, the one is, as it were, wild, the other cultivated, so that, owing to the moisture that accrues to it from being grown in gardens, it also moderately stimulates towards sexual intercourse. This is common to all things that partake of a half-digested and flatulent moisture. On account of such a mixture of the herb, some also apply it with barley meal upon abscesses, which kalaminthe cannot do, because it heats and dries more violently than such things require. It also has in itself something bitter and acerbic, and by the bitter it destroys worms, while by the acerbic, when drunk with oxykraton (vinegar-and-water), it checks recent bringings-up of blood. 6.8.3 [γ΄. Περὶ θέρμου.] Θέρμος, ἐσθίεται μὲν ἑψηθείς τε καὶ πολλαῖς ἡμέραις, ἐναποθέμενος ὕδατι τὴν πικρότητα, καὶ γίνεται τηνικαῦτα τροφὴ παχύχυμος. ὡς φάρμακον δὲ ὁ μὲν τοιοῦτος ἐκ τῶν ἐμπλαστικῶν ἐστιν, ὁ δὲ τὴν σύμφυτον πικρότητα ἔχων ῥυπτικός τε καὶ διαφορητικὸς ὑπάρχει. ἀναιρεῖ δὲ καὶ ἕλμινθας ἐπιπλαττόμενός τε καὶ μετὰ μέλιτος ἐκλειχόμενος ἢ μετ’ ὀξυκράτου πινόμενος, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ ἀφέψημα αὐτοῦ τὰς ἕλμινθας ἐκβάλλειν πέφυκε. καὶ μέν γε καὶ καταντλούμενον ἔξωθεν ὀνίνησιν ἀλφοὺς, ἀχῶρας, ἐξανθήματα, ψώρας, γαγγραίνας, ἕλκη κακοήθη, τὰ μὲν τῷ ῥύπτειν, τὰ δὲ τῷ διαφορεῖν καὶ ξηραίνειν ἀδήκτως. ἐκκαθαίρει δὲ καὶ ἧπαρ καὶ σπλῆνα, μετὰ πηγάνου καὶ πεπέρεως ἡδονῆς ἕνεκα λαμβανόμενον. ἐπισπᾶται δὲ καὶ καταμήνια καὶ ἔμβρυα, σὺν σμύρνῃ καὶ μέλιτι προστιθέμενον. ἔστι δὲ καὶ τὸ ἄλευρον τῶν θέρμων ἀδήκτως διαφορητικόν. οὐ γὰρ τὰ πελιδνὰ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ χοιράδας καὶ φύματα σκληρὰ θεραπεύει, ἐν ὄξει δ’ ἑψεῖν αὐτὸ χρὴ τηνικαῦτα, ἢ ὀξυμέλιτι, ἢ ὀξυκράτῳ, κατά τε τὰς κράσεις δηλονότι τῶν καμνόντων καὶ τοῦ πάθους τὴν διαφορὰν ἐξευρίσκοντα τὸ δέον. οὐκ ἔστι δὲ τῆς προκειμένης νῦν ἡμῖν πραγματείας τὰ τοιαῦτα διαιρεῖσθαι. διαφορεῖ δὲ καὶ τὰ πελιδνά· καὶ τἄλλα ὅσα πρόσθεν εἴρηται τὸ ἀφέψημα δρᾷν, πάντα καὶ τὸ ἄλευρον ἐργάζεσθαι πέφυκε. καταπλάσσουσι δ’ ἔνιοι καὶ τοὺς ἰσχιαδικοὺς αὐτῷ.
Rendering A (fable-5-1)
6.8.3 [3. On the lupin.] The lupin is eaten after it has been boiled and has, over many days, deposited its bitterness in water, and at that point it becomes a food of thick humour. As a drug, however, the lupin of this kind belongs among the clogging agents, whereas the one which retains its innate bitterness is cleansing and dispersing. It also destroys worms, both when applied as a plaster and when licked up with honey or drunk with oxykraton (diluted vinegar); and indeed its decoction too is of a nature to expel worms. And moreover, when poured over externally it benefits alphoi, achores, eruptions, psorai, gangrenes and malignant ulcers, some by cleansing, others by dispersing and drying without biting. It also cleanses out the liver and the spleen, when taken with rue and pepper for the sake of pleasantness. It also draws down the menses and embryos, when applied as a pessary with myrrh and honey. The flour of lupins is likewise dispersing without biting. For it treats not only livid parts but also scrofulous swellings (choirades) and hard tumours (phymata); in that case, however, one must boil it in vinegar, or in oxymel, or in oxykraton, finding out, evidently, what is required according to the mixtures of the patients and the difference of the affection. But it is not the task of the treatise now before us to make such distinctions. It also disperses livid parts; and all the other things which the decoction was said above to do, the flour too is of a nature to accomplish. Some also apply it as a cataplasm to those suffering from sciatica.

6.8.3 [3. On the lupine.] The lupine is eaten when it has been boiled and has, over many days, deposited its bitterness in water; it then becomes a food of thick humours. As a drug, the lupine so treated belongs among the clogging drugs, whereas the one that keeps its innate bitterness is cleansing and dispersing. It also kills worms, whether applied as a plaster, licked up with honey, or drunk with oxycrate. Its decoction, too, is by nature able to expel worms. Moreover, poured over the body from outside, it benefits alphoi, achores, exanthemata, psorai, gangrainai and malignant ulcers, some by cleansing, others by dispersing and drying without biting. It also thoroughly purges liver and spleen when taken with rue and pepper for the sake of pleasantness. It also draws out the menses and embryos when applied with myrrh and honey. The meal of lupines is also dispersing without biting. For it treats not only livid marks but also choirades and hard phymata. In that case one must boil it in vinegar, or oxymel, or oxycrate, finding out what is required evidently according to the mixtures of the patients and the difference of the affection. But it is not the business of the treatise now before us to distinguish such matters. It also disperses livid marks; and all the other things that the decoction was said above to do, the meal too is by nature able to effect. Some also apply it as a cataplasm to sufferers from sciatica.

6.8.6 [6. On lettuce.] Lettuce is a moist and cold vegetable, though not in the extreme degree—for then it would not have been edible—but more or less, as one might say, to the degree of the power, or rather the coldness, of spring waters. For this reason it is suitable for hot inflammations and for the small and slight cases of erysipelas, though it is not capable of sufficing against the greater ones. It is also a food that allays thirst. Its seed, taken in drink, checks gonorrhoeas (seminal fluxes), whence it is also given to those who have nocturnal emissions. So too the seed of the wild lettuce, whose juice they also collect: it cleanses away argema and mistiness (achlys) of the eye, and it is also applied, smeared on with woman's milk, against epikaumata (burn-like ulcers of the eye).

6.8.6 [6. On lettuce.] Lettuce is a moist and cold vegetable, though not extremely so, for then it would not be edible. Rather, it has, so to speak, chiefly the power, or coldness, of spring waters. For this reason it is suited to hot inflammations and to the small and mild among the cases of erysipelas, but it is not able to cope with the larger ones. It is also a thirst-allaying food. Its seed, when drunk, checks seminal flux, and so it is also given to those who have wet dreams. So too does the seed of the wild lettuce, whose juice people also collect; smeared on with woman's milk, it cleans away argema and achlys, and it serves for epicaumata.

6.9.2 [2. On mistletoe.] Mistletoe is composed for the most part of airy and watery substance that is hot, and to the least degree of earthy substance. At any rate the pungent in it is greater than the bitter, and accordingly its actions too are in keeping with its substance. For it draws moistures forcefully out of the depth, not only the thin ones but also the thicker ones, and these it melts down and disperses. It is one of those drugs that do not heat immediately after the first application, but require time, like thapsia. This too has been said earlier, that it is a property of drugs that are hot in power, whenever they have abundant superfluous moisture.

6.9.2 [2. On birdlime.] Birdlime (ixos) is composed of a very large amount of airy and watery substance, which is hot, and a very small amount of earthy substance. At any rate, the pungent in it is greater than the bitter, and accordingly its effects too correspond to its substance. For it powerfully draws moistures out of the depth, not only the thin ones but also the thicker ones, and it both diffuses and disperses them. It is one of those drugs that do not heat at once, after the first application, but require time, like thapsia. This was also said earlier: it is a property of drugs that are hot in power when they contain abundant residual moisture.

6.9.5 [5. On hippomarathron.] Hippomarathron (horse-fennel): this will be spoken of together with fennel. 6.9.6 [6. On woad.] Woad (isatis): the cultivated kind, which the dyers use, is of a strongly drying power, yet not at all biting; for it is at once bitter and astringent. For these reasons it also glues together even the large wounds of hard bodies, even if they are in the heads of the muscles, and it is beneficially plastered upon haemorrhaging parts, and it wonderfully disperses and at the same time represses oedematous swellings, and it wonderfully withstands all malignant ulcers, whether they are putrefying or being eroded. But if at any time it should appear stronger than the nature of the patient, one must mix with its leaves, finely ground, either bread or barley meal or wheat meal or barley groats, according to the predominant condition in each case. The wild woad, however, has something pungent, already clearly perceptible both in taste and in action, and on this account, being more drying than the cultivated kind, it withstands moist putrefactions more strongly, but in the other respects mentioned above it is worse, for it now dries more immoderately and with biting; and such parts become irritated and inflamed. But because of the strength of its power it is also useful for those suffering in the spleen, where the other kind is not yet of any help.

Περὶ ἰτέας.] Ἰτέας χρήσαιτο μὲν ἄν τις καὶ τοῖς φύλλοις εἰς τραυμάτων ἐναίμων κόλλησιν, οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ τῷ ἄνθει μάλιστ’ αὐτῆς ἅπαντες σχεδὸν οἱ ἰατροὶ χρῶνται πρὸς ἐμπλάστρου ξηραινούσης σκευασίαν. ἔστι γὰρ ἡ δύναμις αὐτῶν ξηραντικὴ καὶ ἄδηκτος, ἔχει δὲ καὶ στύψιν. ἔνιοι δὲ καὶ χυλὸν ἐξ αὐτῶν ποιοῦντες, ἄδηκτον καὶ ξηραῖνον ἴσχουσι φάρμακον εἰς πολλὰ χρήσιμον. οὐδὲν γάρ ἐστι πολυχρηστότερον ἀδήκτου καὶ ξηραίνοντος φαρμάκου, στύφοντος ὀλίγον, ὡς κᾀν τοῖς περὶ συνθέσεως τῶν φαρμάκων ἀκριβέστερον δειχθήσεται. καὶ ὁ φλοιὸς δὲ τοῦ δένδρου παραπλήσιος ὑπάρχει τῇ τε τῶν ἀνθῶν καὶ τῶν φύλλων δυνάμει, πλὴν ὅσα ξηρότερός ἐστι τὴν κρᾶσιν, ὥσπερ ἀμέλει καὶ πάντες οἱ φλοιοί. ἀλλὰ τοῦτόν γε καίουσιν ἔνιοι καὶ χρῶνται τῇ τέφρᾳ πρὸς ὅσα περ ἂν ἰσχυρῶς δέωνται ξηραίνειν. τοὺς γοῦν καλουμένους ἥλους καὶ τύλους, ἔτι τε μυρμηκίας ἐξαίρουσιν αὐτὴν δεύοντες ὄξει δριμεῖ. ἔνιοι δὲ κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς ἀνθήσεως ἐντέμνοντες τὸν φλοιὸν, ὀπὸν ἀθροίζουσί τινα καὶ χρῶνται πρὸς τὰ ταῖς κόραις ἐπισκοτοῦντα, ῥυπτικῷ τε ἅμα καὶ λεπτομερεῖ φαρμάκῳ. χρήσαιτο δ’ ἄν τις καὶ εἰς ἄλλα πολλὰ τοιούτῳ γε ὄντι αὐτῷ. ΓΑΛΗΝΟΥ ΠΕΡΙ ΤΗς ΤΩΝ ΑΠΛΩΝ ΦΑΡΜΑΚΩΝ ΚΡΑΣΕΩς ΚΑΙ ΔΥΝΑΜΕΩς ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ Η. Προοίμιον. Ἕβδομον τοῦτο περὶ τῆς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεως ὑπόμνημα γράφοντες ἀναγκαῖον ἡγούμεθα προειπεῖν ὡς μόνοις ἔσοιτο σαφὲς, ὅσοι τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ὡμίλησαν οὐκ ἐν παρέργῳ, τοὺς δ’ ἄλλους ἡγοῦμαι παρακούσεσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ μαθήσεσθαί τι τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ λεχθησομένων καὶ αὐτούς τε σφαλήσεσθαι καὶ ἡμᾶς ἴσως ἐπηρεάσειν, ὡς οὐκ ὀρθῶς τινα γράφοντας. ὅσοι μὲν οὖν σώφρονές εἰσιν οἶδ’ ὅτι πεισθήσονται, καὶ εἴπερ ὅλως πεφροντίκασι τῆς προκειμένης θεωρίας, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς ἀναλέξονται τὴν ὅλην πραγματείαν· ὅσοι δὲ περίεργοι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλομαθεῖς ὑπάρχουσιν, ἀπειθήσουσι τῇ προσρήσει, καὶ οὐδὲν ἴσως θαυμαστὸν, εἴ γε καὶ μυστηρίων βίβλους ἐτόλμησαν ἔνιοι τῶν ἀμυήτων ἀναγινώσκειν. ἀλλ’ οὔτ’ ἐκείνας ἔγραψαν οἱ γράψαντες τοῖς βεβήλοις οὔτ’ ἐγὼ ταῦτα τοῖς μήπω περὶ τὰ πρῶτα γεγυμνασμένοις. εἰρήσονται δ’ ἐν τούτῳ τῷ βιβλίῳ καὶ τῷ μετ’ αὐτὸ τῶν ὑπολοίπων φυτῶν αἱ πρῶται δυνάμεις, τὴν τάξιν τῆς διδασκαλίας κᾀνταῦθα κατὰ τὴν τάξιν τῶν γραμμάτων ποιησαμένων ἡμῶν, ἀφ’ ὧν ἄρχονται. ἐν μὲν οὖν τῷ πρὸ τοῦδε μέχρι τοῦ ι προήλθομεν· ἐνταυθοῖ δὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ κ ποιησόμεθα τοσοῦτον ἔτι προαναμνήσαντες, ὡς εἰς τὰς προαποδεδειγμένας ἀρχὰς ἀνάξομεν ἅπαντα· τῷ γὰρ ἐπὶ τοσόνδε θερμὸν ἢ ψυχρὸν, ἢ ὑγρὸν ἢ ξηρὸν, ἢ λεπτομερὲς ἢ παχυμερὲς ὑπάρχειν ἕκαστον τῶν φαρμάκων αἱ διαφοραὶ τῶν κατὰ μέρος ἐνεργειῶν αὐτῶν γίγνονται, τὸ δ’ ἐπὶ τοσόνδε προήκειν ἐν ἑκάστῳ τῶν προειρημένων ἄῤῥητόν ἐστι πρός γε τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην ἀλήθειαν. ἀλλ’ ἡμεῖς καὶ τοῦτο περιλαβεῖν ἐπειράθημεν ὅροις σαφέσιν, ἱκανοῖς εἰς τὴν χρείαν τῆς τέχνης, ἓν μὲν εἶναι γένος φαρμάκων ἐπιδείξαντες εἰς ὁμοίαν τοῖς σώμασιν ἡμῶν ἀφικνούμενον κρᾶσιν, ἐπειδὰν ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν αὐτοῖς θερμότητος ἀρχήν τινα δέξηται μεταβολῆς τε καὶ ἀλλοιώσεως, ἕτερον δὲ θερμότερον ᾖ καθ’ ἡμᾶς γιγνόμενον, οὗ τέτταρας ἔδοξε ποιήσασθαι τάξεις· πρώτην μὲν τὴν ἀσαφῆ πρὸς αἴσθησιν, ὡς λόγου δεῖσθαι τοῦ φωράσαντος, ἑτέραν δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτῇ δευτέραν, ἤδη πως σαφῆ πρὸς αἴσθησιν, ἄλλην δὲ τρίτην θερμαίνουσαν μὲν ἰσχυρῶς, οὐ μὴν ἤδη γέ πως καίουσαν, ἐφ’ ᾗ τετάρτην τε καὶ ὑστάτην τὴν καυστικήν. οὕτω δὲ καὶ τῶν ψυχόντων πρώτην μὲν τὴν τάξιν τῶν λόγου δεομένων εἰς ἀπόδειξιν τοῦ ψύχειν, δευτέραν δὲ τῶν αἰσθητῶς ψυχόντων, καὶ τρίτην τῶν ἰσχυρῶς, καὶ τετάρτην τῶν νεκρούντων. ἀνάλογον δὲ ταύταις καὶ περὶ τῶν ὑγραινόντων καὶ ξηραινόντων.

6.9.8 [8. On willow.] One might indeed use the leaves of the willow too for the gluing together of bloody wounds; nevertheless it is its flower above all that almost all physicians use for the preparation of a drying plaster. For their power is drying and non-biting, and it also has astringency. Some, moreover, by making a juice from them, obtain a non-biting and drying drug useful for many purposes. For nothing is of more manifold use than a non-biting and drying drug that is slightly astringent, as will be shown more precisely in the books on the composition of drugs. The bark of the tree, too, is closely similar in power to that of the flowers and of the leaves, except insofar as it is drier in mixture, as of course are all barks. But some burn this and use the ash for whatever they need to dry strongly. At any rate they remove the so-called corns and calluses, and myrmekiai as well, by soaking it with pungent vinegar. Others, incising the bark at the season of flowering, collect a certain sap and use it against the things that darken the pupils, it being a drug at once cleansing and fine-particled. And one might use it, being of such a nature, for many other things as well. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK Η. Preface. In writing this seventh treatise on the power of simple drugs, we think it necessary to say in advance that it will be clear only to those who have engaged with the preceding ones not in a cursory way; the others, I think, will misunderstand rather than learn anything of what is to be said in it, and will both go astray themselves and perhaps slander us, as if we were writing some things incorrectly. Now those who are sensible, I know, will be persuaded, and if they have any concern at all for the theory before us, will read through the whole treatise from the beginning; but those who are meddlesome rather than fond of learning will disobey the admonition, and perhaps that is nothing surprising, if indeed some of the uninitiated have even dared to read books of the mysteries. But neither did those who wrote those books write them for the profane, nor do I write these things for those not yet exercised in the first principles. In this book and the one after it there will be set out the primary powers of the remaining plants, we having here too arranged the order of instruction according to the order of the letters with which they begin. In the book before this one, then, we proceeded as far as iota; here we shall make our beginning from kappa, after first recalling only this much further, that we shall refer everything to the principles previously demonstrated. For it is by each of the drugs being hot or cold, or wet or dry, or fine-particled or coarse-particled to such-and-such a degree that the differences of their particular activities arise; but the advancing to such-and-such a degree in each of the aforesaid is inexpressible, at least with respect to the most exact truth. Yet we have attempted to encompass this too within clear boundaries, sufficient for the use of the art, by showing that one class of drugs is that which arrives at a mixture similar to our bodies, once it has received from the heat in them some beginning of change and alteration; another is that which becomes hotter than what is in us, of which we thought fit to make four orders: the first, that which is unclear to sense, so as to require reasoning to detect it; another after it, the second, already in some way clear to sense; another, the third, heating strongly but not yet in any way burning; and after it the fourth and last, the caustic. So too of cooling drugs: the first order is that of those requiring reasoning for the demonstration that they cool; the second, of those cooling perceptibly; the third, of those cooling strongly; and the fourth, of those that deaden. And analogously to these also with regard to moistening and drying drugs.

6.9.8 [8. On willow.] One might use the leaves of the willow as well for the agglutination of bloody wounds; nevertheless, it is its flower above all that almost all physicians use for the preparation of a drying plaster. For the power of these is drying and non-biting, and it also has astringency. Some also make a juice from them and so obtain a non-biting and drying drug, useful for many purposes. For nothing is of more varied use than a non-biting and drying drug that is slightly astringent, as will be shown more precisely in the books on the composition of drugs. The bark of the tree is also similar to the power of the flowers and of the leaves, except in so far as it is drier in mixture, as indeed are all barks. Some burn this bark and use the ash for whatever needs to be dried strongly. For instance, they remove the so-called nails (corns) and calluses, and also warts, by moistening it with pungent vinegar. Some, incising the bark at the time of flowering, collect a certain sap and use it for things that darken the pupils, as a drug at once cleansing and fine-particled. One might also use it for many other things, since it is of such a kind. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK VIII. Preface. In writing this seventh treatise on the power of simple drugs, we think it necessary to state at the outset that it will be clear only to those who have studied the preceding books, and not as a side matter. The others, I think, will misunderstand rather than learn anything of what is to be said in it; they will go astray themselves, and will perhaps abuse us for writing certain things incorrectly. Those who are sensible, I know, will be persuaded, and if they have cared at all for the theory at hand, they will read the whole treatise from the beginning. But those who are meddlesome rather than eager to learn will disregard this advance notice, and perhaps this is nothing surprising, since some of the uninitiated have even dared to read books of the mysteries. But those who wrote those books did not write them for the profane, nor do I write these for those not yet trained in the first matters. In this book and in the one after it the primary powers of the remaining plants will be stated. Here too we have arranged the order of the teaching according to the order of the letters with which their names begin. In the book before this one we advanced as far as iota; here we shall begin from kappa. First we recall only this much: that we shall refer everything back to the principles demonstrated earlier. For the differences in the particular activities of each drug arise from its being hot or cold, moist or dry, fine-particled or coarse-particled to such-and-such a degree. But how far it advances in each of the aforementioned qualities cannot be expressed, at least with respect to the most precise truth. Yet we have tried to circumscribe this too with clear limits, sufficient for the use of the art. We showed that there is one class of drugs that arrives at a mixture similar to our bodies, once it has received from the heat in them some beginning of change and alteration. There is another class that becomes hotter in relation to us, and of this it seemed good to make four orders. The first is unclear to sense perception, so as to need reason to detect it. A second follows it, already in some way clear to sense perception. A third heats strongly, yet does not yet in any way burn. After it comes the fourth and last, the caustic. So too with the cooling drugs: the first order is of those that need reason to demonstrate that they cool, the second of those that cool perceptibly, the third of those that cool strongly, and the fourth of those that mortify. The moistening and drying drugs are treated analogously to these.
